📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On Friday, a petition to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO of Nvidia began circulating on social media, and by Monday it listed some notable signatories, including Elon Musk and several influential Nvidia researchers. But comb through the more than 115,000 names and you’ll notice a significant faction of Huang’s supporters—higher-ups from Hugging Face, a hub for sharing AI models, and venture capital firms Andreessen Horowitz and Sequoia Capital—come from a particular slice of the tech world.

In a recent development, these names have a vested interest in the development of open-source AI, models that, unlike ChatGPT or Claude, can be downloaded and run independent of large tech companies. Supporters of such models say that concentrating AI in the hands of a few powerful companies will leave everyone else worse off (a concern that wouldn’t sound out of place among the AI industry's critics on the left, if so many open-source advocates weren’t also venture capitalists who stand to profit when startups can build on cheaper AI without paying Substantial Tech).

Industry observers note that huang had become a sort of ringleader for those who defend open source to policymakers against concerns that such models come with no guardrails and cede AI leadership to China, where the most powerful and popular open-source models are created. They now want their most influential voice returned to his post.

Sources indicate that but it’s not just Huang’s extramarital affairs that threaten his (and Nvidia’s) credibility as an advocate for open-source AI. Latest research into China’s startups using Nvidia’s chips, and a new rule from the US Department of Commerce announced Monday, could deal a blow to both the movement’s reputation and its technical progress.

On Thursday, the day Huang resigned, ex-OpenAI researcher Will DePue published findings online suggesting that China’s AI companies had far more access to Nvidia’s advanced Blackwell chips than previously estimated. China is banned from accessing Nvidia’s most cutting-edge chips to help protect America’s AI lead.

It’s unclear how they would have gained access to the chips. DePue claims the results were verified by senior researchers at OpenAI and Anthropic, but an independent analysis has not confirmed the results. (DePue did not respond to a request for an interview. Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment.).

The findings do not establish that Nvidia helped Chinese companies obtain the chips, and the broader problem of chip smuggling was already known to extend well beyond Nvidia’s control.

But in suggesting that Nvidia may have profited from the rise of Chinese AI startups, whose models are increasingly being used by American companies instead of domestic alternatives, the findings do leave Huang in an awkward position. He has championed open-source AI as a way to strengthen American technological leadership. “Without open source, startups can’t thrive, university researchers can’t do research, you can’t teach AI, scientists can’t use AI,” he said last December during a talk about helping the US win the AI race against China.

Industry observers note that it also makes the idea of reinstating Huang even more of a long shot. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent even mentioned last week that Nvidia should not consider someone from inside the company to replace him. The latest findings lower Huang’s chances further.

What happens next? Nvidia announced in September it would acquire Hugging Face for nearly $13 billion. Its support for open source also serves a straightforward financial interest: The more businesses that build their own models instead of forking over money to Anthropic and OpenAI, the more chips Nvidia can sell.

Industry observers note that but a fresh rule from the US Department of Commerce could mean the models popular on Hugging Face will soon stop getting smarter. The rule aims to prevent Chinese companies from training models on Nvidia chips that they can’t own directly, but that they can access remotely in data centers in countries like Malaysia—a workaround that has helped China’s open-source models get so good.

The open-source world rallied around Huang because of his influence on policymakers. That was notable, since the rise of China’s open-source models has splintered some in Trump’s orbit. If Huang is out, who is next?

International investigation using trove of leaked internal data allegedly shows German bank overlooked compliance concerns to safeguard profits.

Deutsche Bank reportedly dismissed warnings about its dealings with risky clients, including high-profile Russian oligarchs, to protect profits, the findings of an investigation into a trove of leaked bank documents indicate.

A leak of 15m internal files is reported to show that the troubled German bank repeatedly ignored concerns by its compliance officers about its risk-taking, despite having already been caught being used to launder billions of dollars for Russian criminals, spies and oligarchs between 2010 and 2015.

The investigations, which were published by media outlets including Der Spiegel, the Financial Times, the Newly introduced York Times and Le Monde, will represent a fresh blow for Deutsche Bank, which has struggled to repair its reputation after a number of scandals and dealings with controversial clients including the US president, Donald Trump, and the sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

In a recent development, deutsche Bank stated on Tuesday that the concerns raised in the investigations “date back many years, in some cases as much as two decades” and had been addressed by its leadership. “Where relevant, we reviewed these matters at the time and worked closely with regulators.”.

However, the reports suggested Deutsche Bank prioritised profit ahead of internal controls, and continued to expand its Russian business until 2021, despite warnings from internal compliance officers and growing geopolitical tensions between Nato allies and Moscow.

Deutsche Bank allegedly resisted pulling out of Russia even after the Kremlin released a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, before the bank did a U-turn and exiting the country in March that year.

In a recent development, the investigations suggested Deutsche Bank was driven by competitive pressure, including from American banks, and that its chief executive, Christian Sewing, pursued a growth strategy that involved doing business with a list of customers known as its “most sensitive clients”. That covered roughly 50 corporate clients ranked by how close they were to the Kremlin, and other potential risks including financial crime, according to the Financial Times.

Some names allegedly on that list included: Russia’s state-owned gas organization Gazprom; petrochemicals group Sibur; and oligarchs including the aluminium magnate Oleg Deripaska, the report noted.

In a recent development, outside its Russian dealings, the German lender is facing fresh scrutiny for allegedly processing almost $600m (£454m) of suspicious payments linked to Epstein, much higher than previously known. Deutsche mentioned it “regrets [its] historical relationship” with Epstein and that it had made “considerable investments in strengthening controls”.

The lender is also accused of accidentally leaking Trump’s tax documents to another client during his first term in office, which Deutsche Bank allegedly kept secret from the White House. Deutsche Bank said it did not comment on former or existing client relationships. Deutsche Bank cut ties with Trump in 2021.

The reports prompted a 4% drop in Deutsche Bank’s German-listed shares on Tuesday.

Deutsche Bank issued a public statement in response to the investigation on Tuesday, saying it had “gone through a fundamental transformation” under Sewing.

Recent findings suggest that “We made substantial investments in our control environment while restoring sustainable profitability, as evidenced by record profits in 2025 as well as in recent quarters. This involved €7bn of direct investments in our control environment between 2019 and 2025.”.

The bank added: “We remain committed to ensuring continuous enhancements of our control environment and a culture of integrity and completing any outstanding remediation.”.

“Regardless of how the information was obtained, it includes confidential information about clients, employees and other third parties, which remains legally protected. We have acted, and will continue to act, decisively to protect this,” the bank noted.

#12462. How to put your iPad in recovery mode (with and without a home button)

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (543 w)

Gadgets ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Engadget ↗ Open Full Page

How to put your iPad in recovery mode (with and without a home button)

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (543 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A failed update or a forgotten passcode doesn't have to mean the end of your iPad.
  • It has been revealed that many iPad problems can be fixed with a simple restart, but sometimes that's not enough.
  • In a recent development, recovery mode also lets you connect your iPad to your computer to update it, or in the worst-case scenario, restore it to its factory default settings.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A failed update or a forgotten passcode doesn't have to mean the end of your iPad.

It has been revealed that many iPad problems can be fixed with a simple restart, but sometimes that's not enough. Severe issues with the tablet's software can make it completely inoperable, and in these cases, putting the iPad in recovery mode might be your only option.

In a recent development, recovery mode also lets you connect your iPad to your computer to update it, or in the worst-case scenario, restore it to its factory default settings. It's best to save recovery mode for when nothing else works, but when it's needed, it can mean the difference between a bricked iPad and one that works just like new.

There are a few situations when you might want to use recovery mode. Major software updates can sometimes fail, leaving you with a partially installed update that keeps your iPad from turning on. Your iPad might reboot itself continuously, or you might enter the wrong passcode too many times and get locked out. Your computer might also stop recognizing your iPad, or your iPad might show a screen prompting you to connect it to a computer.

To put your iPad in recovery mode, first connect it to your computer with a USB cable, and open Finder on Mac or the Apple Devices app on PC. From here, the process differs based on whether your iPad has a home button or not. If it does, hold the home and the power button down at the same time. Eventually, your iPad screen will go black and then show the Apple logo. Finally, it will show the recovery mode icon: an image of a USB cable connecting to a computer. Now release the buttons.

Recent findings suggest that newer iPads, like the iPad Pro, don't have a home button, so you need to use the power and volume buttons instead. First press and release the volume up button and then the volume down button. Next, press and hold the power button, and keep holding it through the Apple logo until the recovery mode icon appears. Then let go.

At this point, you can use the Finder or Apple Devices on your computer to find your iPad. If the process worked, you should see a pop-up explaining that the iPad needs to be restored or updated. It's best to start with the update option, which will allow your computer to reinstall iPadOS without affecting anything else stored on your device.

Sources indicate that if this option is successful, you'll be able to use your iPad again without losing any data. If it doesn't work, though, you'll have to put it back in recovery mode and choose the restore option. This will restore the iPad to its factory settings, completely erasing your data in the process.

You can restore everything from your most recent backup (if you have enough iCloud storage), but it's a far more disruptive process that should only be used as a last resort. If your iPad still isn't working after trying both options or you can't get it to enter recovery mode, it may be time to get it professionally repaired or shop for a new iPad.

  • The Vulcan rocket is on contract to launch roughly half of the US military’s national security space missions in the next few years, and Sunday’s mission was the first of 38 Vulcan launches booked by Amazon to build out its network of broadband Internet satellites aimed at competing with SpaceX’s Starlink.
  • In a recent development, vulcan is no stranger to close calls, having overcome failures with its strap-on solid rocket boosters on two of its four previous flights.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

United Launch Alliance’s Vulcan rocket and 40 Amazon Leo broadband satellites fell back to Earth minutes after liftoff Sunday, a crushing setback that will ripple across all sectors of the US space industry.

The Vulcan rocket is on contract to launch roughly half of the US military’s national security space missions in the next few years, and Sunday’s mission was the first of 38 Vulcan launches booked by Amazon to build out its network of broadband Internet satellites aimed at competing with SpaceX’s Starlink. Sunday’s failure is expected to ground the rocket for an indefinite period of time.

In a recent development, vulcan is no stranger to close calls, having overcome failures with its strap-on solid rocket boosters on two of its four previous flights. In each case, the rocket corrected for those problems and continued into orbit to deploy its payloads. The incidents triggered monthslong reviews and investigations before ULA could resume Vulcan flights.

Sunday’s launch succumbed to a different kind of failure. The six solid rocket boosters appeared to perform well in the first two minutes after Vulcan’s liftoff from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station, Florida, at 12:40 pm EDT (17:40 UTC).

In a statement, ULA noted the rocket “suffered an anomaly 10 minutes into the flight and failed to deliver the Amazon mission to orbit.” The company said it did not immediately have “any specific data to understand what occurred.”.

It has been revealed that “ULA exists to provide assured access to space for our nation and for the customers who depend on us,” the company said in a statement. “That purpose is why we take on some of the hardest missions in spaceflight, and why we hold ourselves to the standard of mission success. Today, we did not meet that standard.”.

Engineers will investigate the failure to “find the cause, determine the appropriate corrective action, and return to flight as swiftly as possible,” ULA said.

“ULA is committed to full transparency with our customers, and they will have visibility into the investigation process, which utilizes rigorous methodology and corrective action. We will provide further updates when newly introduced information becomes available.”.

The first indications of trouble Sunday appeared to crop up before the 10-minute mark of the flight, the point in time when ULA initially remarked the anomaly occurred.

Multiple sources told Ars the anomaly that impacted the launch occurred in the booster stage of the rocket, not the Centaur V upper stage or the solid rocket boosters. It could not immediately be determined whether the booster stage matter was caused by the two methane-burning BE-4 engines that power it, some other part of the booster that feeds propellant into the engines, or another problem.

Heading northeast from Cape Canaveral, Vulcan jettisoned its spent solid rocket boosters on time, leaving the launcher flying on the power of its twin BE-4 main engines supplied by Blue Origin, Jeff Bezos’ space company. The BE-4s, each designed to produce more than a half-million pounds of thrust, were supposed to shut down just shy of the flight’s five-minute mark. However, they continued firing for at least 30 additional seconds.

Such an overburn could be an indication the booster stage was not performing as expected and operated longer to try to compensate for the underperformance.

Sources indicate that A mission animation on ULA’s broadcast, driven by real-time telemetry data from the rocket, revealed Vulcan start to spin moments after booster engine shutdown. The spin continued through separation of the rocket’s Centaur V upper stage a few seconds later. ULA’s launch commentator confirmed ignition of the Centaur’s two RL10 engines, and the animation showed them vectoring thrust in an apparent attempt to put the rocket back on course.

According to recent reports, ULA ended its live broadcast a few minutes later without discussion of the anomaly. The tech giant then released a statement on social media declaring the launch a failure. This was the first total mission failure for United Launch Alliance since its formation in 2006 with the merger of the rocket divisions of Boeing and Lockheed Martin.

Recent findings suggest that sunday’s incident is bad news for ULA’s two primary customers: Amazon and the US Space Force. It’s also a potential setback for NASA’s Artemis program to return astronauts to the Moon.

First, Amazon. The loss of 40 Amazon Leo satellites onboard the Vulcan rocket is, by itself, a secondary concern next to the inevitable grounding of the tech giant’s primary launch provider. Amazon has 37 more Vulcan releases reserved with ULA, each of which is slated to deliver 40 or more Amazon Leo satellites to orbit.

The Amazon Leo constellation today consists of 396 satellites, a fraction of the network’s planned total of 3,292 first-generation spacecraft. Amazon officials told Ars in October that the tech giant has enough satellites to start initial commercial Internet service by the end of the year, but more launches are required to realize the network’s full capacity.

According to recent reports, amazon is setting up its service as the first head-to-head competitor in the consumer satellite broadband market with the Starlink network owned by Elon Musk and SpaceX. OneWeb and other companies also offer Internet connectivity from space, but their business models focus on beaming capacity to traditional telco providers, not directly to consumers.

According to recent reports, previous delays with the Vulcan rocket have kept Amazon satellites on the ground far longer than the company planned. Amazon recently confirmed it manufactured its 1,000th satellite, meaning more than half of its network nodes are sitting in storage. Finally, Amazon was looking forward to ramping up its launch cadence, with Sunday’s launch the first for Amazon Leo on ULA’s Vulcan rocket.

According to recent reports, “There is risk with any launch, and that’s especially true for inaugural missions like LV-01,” Amazon mentioned in a statement. “ULA has been a trusted partner for Amazon, and we believe they’ll learn from this mission and deliver on their long-term looks for Vulcan.”.

Recent findings suggest that amazon made launch bookings with Europe’s Arianespace and Bezos’ Blue Origin at the same time it signed the contract for 38 Vulcan debuts in 2022. Amazon reserved additional launches with Arianespace in September, bringing that tech giant’s total contract to 24 launches for Amazon. Three have debuted so far, and the fourth is set to take off later this month on an Ariane 6 rocket from French Guiana.

Blue Origin’s New Glenn rocket has also encountered setbacks on its early missions. Most recently, a New Glenn rocket exploded during a ground test in Florida in May, knocking Blue Origin’s launch pad offline until at least the end of this year. The New Glenn that exploded was supposed to launch a batch of Amazon Leo satellites, but luckily for Amazon, the payloads were not stacked aboard the rocket at the time.

What’s more, the New Glenn rocket uses a version of the BE-4 engine similar to the one that flies on ULA’s Vulcan rocket. Investigators traced the New Glenn explosion to a faulty valve on one of the booster’s BE-4 engines. If engineers determine a BE-4 was at fault on Sunday’s Vulcan failure, it could stand in the way of Blue Origin returning New Glenn to flight early next year.

In a recent development, that would mean more delays for two of the rockets Amazon needs to get its satellites in orbit. Amazon’s past rocket woes forced officials to contract with SpaceX, Bezos’ chief competitor in the satellite broadband and launch sectors, to use its workhorse Falcon 9 rocket to speed up Amazon Leo deployment. Amazon has 10 more missions booked on SpaceX’s Falcon 9 and will presumably be unable to buy more as SpaceX moves the rocket toward retirement.

In a recent development, it’s a similar story for the Space Force, which relies upon SpaceX and ULA to launch the military’s most sensitive national security satellites. The Space Force in 2025 added Blue Origin’s New Glenn as a third option to launch the country’s critical military payloads.

It has been revealed that vulcan’s earlier delays forced Space Force officials to move six national security rolls out from ULA to SpaceX. Military officials used the swaps to get time-sensitive payloads into space sooner on Falcon 9 or Falcon Heavy, rather than waiting for Vulcan. In exchange, the Space Force awarded a future SpaceX mission to ULA.

Sources indicate that expect more Space Force rocket swaps after Vulcan’s errant launch Sunday. For the foreseeable future, the Pentagon will only increase its already heavy dependence on SpaceX to send US national security satellites to space as military leaders race to keep pace with China’s growing presence in orbit.

But SpaceX has made it clear Falcon 9 and Falcon Heavy won’t be around much longer. Musk’s tech giant is rapidly transitioning to Starship to launch its own Starlink satellites and latest orbiting AI-powered compute platforms. SpaceX has not revealed plans yet to certify Starship for national security missions, a process that would take multiple years.

Sources indicate that amazon will likely have to use the 10 Falcon 9 releases it has already reserved and Europe’s Ariane 6 rocket to add any more Amazon Leo satellites to the network in the coming months. Blue Origin’s New Glenn, once it returns to flight, has a series of backlogged launches for NASA’s Artemis Moon program next year, including key test flights of Blue’s lunar lander to prepare for future human missions. Those Moon lander tests could be pushed back further if the BE-4 engine was at fault for Sunday’s failure.

Recent findings suggest that NASA’s lunar program has another key link to the Vulcan rocket. The space agency recently confirmed it selected a version of ULA’s Centaur upper stage for future flights of NASA’s Space Launch System rocket, the vehicle used for launching astronaut crews to the Moon. The Centaur will replace a more expensive, unproven Boeing upper stage design. NASA officials will want to rule out a problem with the Centaur V upper stage on Sunday’s doomed launch as the agency aims to start flying ULA’s Centaur on SLS missions for crewed lunar flights as soon as 2028.

In a recent development, “Appreciate you rapidly keeping the public and your partners informed,” NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman wrote in reply to ULA’s statement on the Vulcan launch anomaly. “The team at NASA is available to assist in all matters related to the investigation and remediation effort. Artemis, Moon Base, and the nation need ULA. We are in your corner and here to help.”.

Tech Report: Suspected Chinese spy balloon was able to transmit information back to Beijing

📅 03 Apr 2023 | ⏱️ 3 min read (659 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNN

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Chinese spy balloon that transited the US earlier this year was able to capture imagery and collect some signals intelligence from US military sites, a source familiar with the matter tells CNN.
  • The balloon was able to transmit information back to Beijing in real time, the source mentioned, and the US government still does not know for sure whether the Chinese government could wipe the balloon’s data as it received it.
  • Still, the intelligence community has not been overly concerned about the information the balloon was able to gather, the person said, because it is not much more sophisticated than what Chinese satellites are able to glean as they orbit over similar locations.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Chinese spy balloon that transited the US earlier this year was able to capture imagery and collect some signals intelligence from US military sites, a source familiar with the matter tells CNN.

The balloon was able to transmit information back to Beijing in real time, the source mentioned, and the US government still does not know for sure whether the Chinese government could wipe the balloon’s data as it received it. That raises questions about whether there is intelligence the balloon was able to gather that the US still doesn’t know about.

Still, the intelligence community has not been overly concerned about the information the balloon was able to gather, the person said, because it is not much more sophisticated than what Chinese satellites are able to glean as they orbit over similar locations.

A US intelligence official told CNN on Monday that “although analysis of the wreckage of the High Altitude Balloon remains ongoing, thus far, its flight over the United States does not appear to have provided critical fresh insights to the People’s Republic of China.”.

The US also knew what the balloon’s path would be and was able to protect sensitive sites and censor some signals before the balloon was able to pick them up, officials have remarked.

As CNN has reported, the US intelligence community last year developed a method of tracking what it states is a fleet of these Chinese balloons operating across the globe, controlled by the Chinese military.

The FBI is still examining the balloon, but so far officials have been able to glean additional information about how the device worked, including the algorithms used for the balloon’s software and how it is powered and designed.

According to recent reports, CNN has reached out to the National Security Council at the White House and the Pentagon for comment. NBC was first to report on the fresh intelligence.

Sources indicate that the balloon first crossed into US airspace over Alaska in late January before passing through Canada and down into Montana, where it hovered for a few days, leading the US to believe it was trying to surveil sensitive military sites, like Malmstrom Air Force Base in Montana. It was eventually shot down by the US off the East Coast on February 4, and the incident further escalated tensions between Washington and Beijing, including the postponement of a diplomatic visit by US Secretary of State Antony Blinken to China.

A senior State Department official mentioned in February that, as the balloon floated across the US, it “was capable of conducting signals intelligence collection operations.”.

Gen. Glen VanHerck, the commander of US Northern Command and NORAD, remarked at the time that the US “did not assess” that the balloon “presented a significant collection hazard beyond what already exists in actionable technical means from the Chinese.”.

Recent findings suggest that the surveillance program, which includes a number of similar balloons, is in part run out of the small Chinese province of Hainan, officials told CNN. The US does not know the precise size of the fleet of Chinese surveillance balloons, but sources tell CNN that the program has conducted at least two dozen missions over at least five continents in recent years.

Roughly half a dozen of those flights have been within US airspace, although not necessarily over US territory, according to one official familiar with the intelligence.

China has maintained that the balloon was actually just a weather balloon thrown off course, and the US has been assessing the possibility that it was not deliberately maneuvered into the continental US by the Chinese government, CNN has reported.

Still, China did maintain some ability to maneuver the balloon, officials believe. And once the balloon was over Montana, China appeared to take advantage of its position to loiter over sensitive sites and try to collect intelligence.

This story has been updated with additional reporting.

CNN’s Alex Marquardt contributed to this report.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • If you're hoping for a cheap RTX card this November, the memory market has other looks.
  • In a recent development, jensen Huang threw in the towel on November 12, resigning as NVIDIA's CEO after founding the organization more than three decades ago.
  • Recent findings suggest that with Black Friday less than two weeks away, people want to know whether they can get their mitts on some cheap NVIDIA.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you're hoping for a cheap RTX card this November, the memory market has other looks.

In a recent development, jensen Huang threw in the towel on November 12, resigning as NVIDIA's CEO after founding the organization more than three decades ago. NVIDIA's market value subsequently fell below $4 trillion for the first time since July 2025 before the week was out, leaving the market in a state of flux.

Recent findings suggest that with Black Friday less than two weeks away, people want to know whether they can get their mitts on some cheap NVIDIA. While some mean the stock, which closed at around $162 on Friday, others mean the RTX 5080 they've had their eyes on all year. Spoiler alert: only one price has fallen, and it'll take more than a CEO scandal to move the needle on the other.

It has been revealed that NVIDIA's graphics cards were already selling way beyond their list prices before Huang's scandal began, because AI data centers have spent the year swallowing the memory those cards need. The RTX 5080, for example, debuted at $999 and now starts at $1,999. The RTX 5090 was $1,999 at launch and sells at close to $7,000 at the lower end. Black Friday has a long record of barely denting GPU prices, and this year retailers have even less room than usual.

In a recent development, NVIDIA's stock had already dropped by around 20 percent over five straight weeks of losses before its board opened an investigation into Huang on November 8. That included a 9 percent drop following the midterm results and ballot measures that could slow data center construction.

Industry observers note that reports in late October then linked Jensen Huang to Alice Huang, a Singapore-based exec whom U.S. officials reportedly suspect of spying for China. He then admitted to an affair with Alice Huang on November 8. Four days later, Jensen Huang was out as NVIDIA CEO, and by Friday's close the manufacturer had posted six consecutive weekly losses. That's its longest streak since 2012, with roughly $1.7 trillion in market value shed since early October.

HSBC downgraded NVIDIA from buy to hold on November 13, cutting its price target from $365 to $170, arguing that the stock would languish until the organization names a permanent CEO. Colette Kress is acting as interim CEO in the meantime while continuing as CFO, a role she has held since 2013. Shares fell another 3.7 percent in premarket trading on Monday, a day before what will be NVIDIA's first-ever earnings report without Jensen Huang.

Industry observers note that data centers brought in the lion's share of NVIDIA's $96.2 billion in last-quarter revenue, accounting for $89 billion. That leaves $7.2 billion for everything else, gamers included. The cause is that memory makers have been focusing on AI chips, pushing up the price of GDDR7 memory that RTX 50-series cards need.

During the crypto-era shortage of 2021, Ethereum miners were snapping up cards that'd otherwise have gone to gamers, causing prices to balloon. That Black Friday, the best GPU deals were 5 to 10 percent off prices that were themselves already way too high. A year later, the miners were gone. Crypto prices crashed in May 2022, and Ethereum's switch to proof-of-stake that September instantly wiped out GPU mining profitability on the network, yet retailers still sold the RTX 3080 at its $699 list price while calling it a Black Friday deal.

It has been revealed that even without miners competing for stock, Tom's Hardware saw no real GPU deals over the 2023 Black Friday weekend, and in 2024 RTX 4090s were selling above $2,000 against their $1,599 MSRP. By the run-up to last year's Black Friday event, some RTX 50-series cards had settled within $30 of their list prices, but the sales barely had an impact. A PNY RTX 5060 down $20 to $279 made Windows Central's list of NVIDIA deals, while the cheapest RTX 5090 PC Gamer could find was $2,700, $700 over the list price. Those were the best conditions for any potential GPU deals in five years, and they led to discounts measured in tens of dollars.

In a recent development, retailers heading into Black Friday on November 27 are holding RTX 50-series stock bought at wholesale prices that NVIDIA's Chinese board partners raised again in November. Yes, a Black Friday sale could shave some margin off the top, but any deals will still only be a very modest cut at best from record GPU prices. NVIDIA's stock price, meanwhile, will keep reacting to the likes of earnings and the board's choice of successor. Its GPUs, however, answer to the memory market and the data centers buying up all the organization's output.

Walmart's Black Friday sale is arriving in three waves this year, with the first big deals drop kicking off on Nov. 12 and running until Nov. 15. The retailer's ad scans have been live for some time, offering shoppers a sneak peek at what's to come during its early Black Friday sale.

This three-day-long event is just the start, though. The retailer also has a Black Friday sale planned for Nov. 23-29, plus a Cyber Monday sale running from Nov. 30 to Dec. 2. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ukraine has critically damaged the Kerch bridge linking occupied Crimea with Russia in an overnight missile attack, in what Ukrainian officials say is a symbolic blow to the Kremlin.

Photos suggest that a 227-metre road arch span has fallen into the Kerch strait, which connects the Sea of Azov with the Black Sea. The adjacent railway arch span has also sustained damage.

Ukrainian commentators say the massive steel arch cannot easily be replaced. The closure of the bridge means that traffic from Crimea can travel out of the peninsula only via a land corridor through occupied southern Ukraine, vulnerable to Ukrainian drones.

But Russian officials, quoted by Reuters, insisted that damage was only minor, and would be quick to sort out.

Sources indicate that “We have already gathered together the resources, designers, and builders ‌for repair work. We are sorting out logistics challenges with the regional leadership,” Russian deputy prime minister Marat Khusnullin wrote on Telegram.

The bridge has in the past been a key supply route for Russian forces in Ukraine ​and is widely viewed as one of Russian president Vladimir Putin’s signature infrastructure projects.

The overnight strike followed ‌an intensification of ​Russian attacks in the ​past few months on bridges in Ukraine, including in the capital Kyiv.

Elsewhere, EU defence ministers are meeting in Brussels this morning for their latest discussions on Ukraine, followed by the Ukraine defence contact group.

Meanwhile, Germany’s chancellor Friedrich Merz is hosting Finland’s influential Alexander Stubb, two days before a major meeting of the coalition of the willing in Berlin.

They will no doubt offer their reaction to today’s events in Ukraine. I will bring you all the latest.

It’s Tuesday, 17 November 2026, it’s Jakub Krupa here, and this is Europe Live.

Delivery drones are coming. For some with PTSD, that's a terrifying prospect.

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1980 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In August, Amazon announced looks to expand its Prime Air delivery drone program to “nearly 500 cities and towns by the end of 2026.” Combined with similar uncrewed aerial delivery programs from DoorDash and Zipline (in partnership with Uber and Walmart), the expansion suggests that flying robots dropping their payloads onto suburban lawns will soon be commonplace.
  • For many people, delivery drones will be little more than a novelty, occasionally good for a laugh when one does something ridiculous.
  • The use of all manner of weaponized drones in the ongoing war in Ukraine and in Israeli attacks on Lebanon and Gaza has already produced an epidemic of what some mental health professionals have dubbed “dronophobia.” And while relatively few US troops have been targeted by drones flown by Iran, ISIS, and Iran-backed militias throughout the Middle East, even those who have not directly been attacked may experience anxiety simply because of the ample video footage of attacks circulating in news and social media.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In August, Amazon announced looks to expand its Prime Air delivery drone program to “nearly 500 cities and towns by the end of 2026.” Combined with similar uncrewed aerial delivery programs from DoorDash and Zipline (in partnership with Uber and Walmart), the expansion suggests that flying robots dropping their payloads onto suburban lawns will soon be commonplace.

For many people, delivery drones will be little more than a novelty, occasionally good for a laugh when one does something ridiculous. For others, though, their growing use could be a nightmare. As the instant delivery industry clears the last FAA hurdles to rapid deliveries beyond an operator’s line of sight, an increasing number of people worldwide are living with post-traumatic stress disorder or other anxiety-related disorders triggered by drones.

The use of all manner of weaponized drones in the ongoing war in Ukraine and in Israeli attacks on Lebanon and Gaza has already produced an epidemic of what some mental health professionals have dubbed “dronophobia.” And while relatively few US troops have been targeted by drones flown by Iran, ISIS, and Iran-backed militias throughout the Middle East, even those who have not directly been attacked may experience anxiety simply because of the ample video footage of attacks circulating in news and social media.

Combined with broader anxiety about surveillance technologies, artificial intelligence, and things generally falling from the sky, the resulting hypervigilance could result in some unintended deliveries from those Prime Air flying robots.

Drones have been a part of the battlefield in some form since the late 1980s, when the Israeli Defense Forces began using them. From the beginning, they have had a psychological impact on both those in the sights of drone operators and the operators themselves.

Sources indicate that the first military use of drones was for intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance. I witnessed the development of naval drone operations aboard USS Iowa in 1986 and 1987, and for many on the ship at the time, the drones were a curiosity—or, at worst, an annoyance. Our crews spent hours standing by a boat, ready to retrieve crashed drones from the water. But we were helping develop a capability that would eventually lead to Iraqi troops surrendering to the USS Wisconsin‘s drone during the Gulf War. Back then, drones were merely heralds of destruction, acting as forward observers for the Air Force ordnance fired or introduced from elsewhere.

Iraqi troops on Faylaka Island associated the Pioneer RPV with the bombardment they had just experienced from the USS Missouri. When the Wisconsin’s drone flew in to assess the damage, their morale was broken.

It has been revealed that over southern Lebanon, the same kinds of drones were part of what amounted, for some residents, to sonic psychological warfare—the hum of lawnmower-like engines overhead was a reminder of constant surveillance and the ever-present threat of artillery or air strikes. The resulting anxiety intensified as drones began carrying their own weapons and “loitering munitions,” one-way drones designed to fly into targets and explode.

Israel’s continued fight against Hezbollah in Lebanon, along with the US wars in Afghanistan and Iraq, accelerated the evolution of drone warfare and expanded the population experiencing its psychological effects. A Stanford Law study in 2012 of the impact of US drones in Pakistan (PDF) highlighted how drones were destroying the fabric of communities in northwest Pakistan:.

Drones hover twenty-four hours a day over communities in northwest Pakistan, striking homes, vehicles, and public spaces without warning. Their presence terrorizes men, women, and children, giving rise to anxiety and psychological trauma among civilian communities. Those living under drones have to face the constant worry that a deadly strike may be fired at any moment and the knowledge that they are powerless to protect themselves.

That experience has been repeated and amplified in current conflicts in Gaza, Lebanon, and Ukraine. A team of US and Ukrainian psychiatrists has reported that Ukrainian military personnel and civilians who have experienced a drone attack, particularly those injured in one, “are at heightened risk for developing persistent psychological symptoms, a vulnerability intensified by the ongoing threat of repeated attacks.”.

Those symptoms—a “unique hypervigilance behavior with corresponding hyperarousal and avoidance behaviors”—are now referred to by some Ukrainian doctors as “dronophobia.”.

“The distinct hum of an approaching drone, often likened to the swarming of hornets, has itself become a psychological weapon,” noted the team led by Dr. Joseph L. Bonvie of Massachusetts General Hospital. “The escalating pitch as a drone draws near elicits fear and helplessness even before an attack.”.

Industry observers note that similar symptoms have been reported in women and children in Gaza, where Israeli drone strikes have been persistent. In consultations with 19 patients in Gaza, “all patients reported an intense phobic reaction to the acoustic signature of drones (the ‘zannana’), associated with imminent bombing and death, manifesting as full-blown panic attacks,” wrote Dr. Mohammad Abu Slaih, a Jordanian psychiatrist, in an article for European Psychiatry. “Three children developed a specific fear of looking at the sky. “.

The Iranian drone attacks on Gulf states, while hardly comparable to what Gaza has endured, have had a broad impact on civilians in the United Arab Emirates and other countries in the region, disrupting sleep, causing fatigue, and fueling anticipatory anxiety as people wait for the next drone to strike.

That anxiety is common across populations exposed to drone warfare. The US Army Training and Doctrine Command (TRADOC) has compared drones’ potential to induce PTSD to the “shell shock” of World War I and the “battle fatigue” of World War II, noting that the “fear and stress from (the sound of) near-persistent drone presence creates anticipatory anxiety… Fears can persist beyond the drone’s presence, enhancing a soldier’s anxiety even when out of harm’s way.”.

Sources indicate that the use of drone video by both Russia and Ukraine as a psychological warfare tool extends the impact of drones beyond those who experience attacks firsthand. Footage of attacks on individual soldiers has been posted on social media to spread anxiety among opposing forces, sometimes going viral and exposing thousands of other people to the attacks. Ukrainian military units often publish first-person-view videos of drones chasing down Russian soldiers, complete with horror-film-styled soundtracks.

According to Neda Gould, an associate professor of psychiatry and behavioral sciences at Johns Hopkins School of Medicine, that aspect sets drone-induced PTSD apart from other types of the disorder. In an interview with Psychiatry Online, Gould remarked social media could amplify trauma because “not only does the soldier have to grapple with the PTSD-related consequences of the attack itself, but they may also relive the experience in a way that is completely out of their control,” especially when social media comments express support for the attacks.

Sources indicate that the US military has grappled with drone-induced PTSD and other mental health symptoms over the past 15 years. The first signs of stress for American troops, however, came from drone operators themselves.

In 2014, a team of researchers led by a US Air Force psychologist found that 4.3 percent of Air Force drone operators displayed “a pattern of symptoms of moderate to extreme level of severity” associated with PTSD. More recent studies have found that drone operators are just as likely to experience PTSD symptoms as members of aircrews deployed to war zones. Differences in how crews operate between manned combat aircraft and unmanned systems crews may even put drone operators at greater risk of psychological impact.

The dual psychological impact of drone warfare was aptly demonstrated by Killbox, a video artwork and “game” that presents two perspectives: those of a drone operator and a child on the ground. Playing it leaves many people deeply saddened, offering a glimpse of the moral injury some drone operators have experienced after their missions.

US troops are no longer just the ones behind the screens, however. Beginning with operations against ISIS, US troops have faced increasingly sophisticated drone warfare, starting with grenades dropped by ISIS-operated consumer quadcopter drones in 2017. Since then, Iranian-built drones, some based on reverse-engineered technology from downed US drones, have been used against US troops and ships by Iran and Iranian-backed militias in Yemen and Iraq. Among these is the Shahed, a long-range attack drone that Iran has sold in large numbers to Russia for its war on Ukraine.

The US Army TRADOC report also recognized that the psychological effects of drone attacks can reach further than those wounded in attacks, and even beyond the units that encounter them, saying:.

Recent findings suggest that drones amplify the uncertainties of war because rear areas are less secure as long-range drones extend danger zones beyond that of artillery and rockets. The feeling of nowhere being safe exacerbates anxiety even when drones are not present.

While little public data is available on drone-induced PTSD among US veterans, evidence suggests that drones could also affect people with PTSD stemming from other kinds of trauma. The sound of a drone, its shadow, a glimpse of one in peripheral vision, or other stimuli from drones could trigger hypervigilance because of their unexpectedness, their similarity to other triggering stimuli, or a range of other factors.

Even for those who have not experienced drone attacks, the presence of an uncrewed aircraft can cause anxiety. Drones purportedly operated by the Department of Homeland Security in Minneapolis earlier this year appeared to be used not just for surveillance of targets of Immigration and Customs Enforcement but also to intimidate individuals who had been tracking ICE activity.

The expanding use of drones by law enforcement organizations in the US as part of “drone first responder” programs has exposed an increasing number of Americans to drone surveillance, with over 1,000 agencies applying for FAA waivers for drone operations as of February 2026, based on data from the Electronic Frontier Foundation. Combined with news reports about drone attacks and foreign governments’ use of drones, the disquiet of drone propeller noises and blinking lights in the sky has already created a War of the Worlds level of dronophobia.

Over the past two years, several drone incidents have been linked, or suspected of being linked, to state-actor espionage, with a surge in reports in November and December of 2024. Three occurred in Southern California, including a drone flyover of Vandenberg Air Force Base as a National Reconnaissance Office payload was being loaded ont0 a SpaceX rocket. A Chinese national was charged in the case and arrested while attempting to leave the country. Other cases in the US were officially downplayed as posing no security threat.

According to recent reports, in November 2024, incidents in the UK centered on multiple air bases used by the US, including incursions near RAF Fairford, the base recently allegedly targeted in a plot that the British government attributed to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. Similar incursions occurred in Germany.

Around the same time, a rash of civilian “drone sightings” across the US emerged, particularly in Upcoming Jersey. Anxiety grew further after a Republican New Jersey congressman claimed there was an “Iranian drone mothership.” Segments of the population were ready to shoot down drones themselves.

Many of these sightings turned out to be crewed aircraft or helicopters, toy drones, or, in very few cases, authorized commercial drone flights. Former Maryland Governor Larry Hogan even reported seeing dozens of large drones above his house, only for others to quickly point out that the objects were actually the constellation Orion.

PTSD is a treatable condition, and coping strategies can help people manage triggers. But severe PTSD can be extremely debilitating, and research into the effects of drones on PTSD remains limited. It’s still unclear how well survivors of drone attacks will be able to process the fears and traumatic memories associated with drones, especially if the aircraft become a pervasive part of daily life.

I, for one, won’t be placing any Prime Air orders anytime soon.

Best Laptops (2026): My Top Recommendations After Testing Hundreds
