📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that I’ve been reviewing laptops for well over a decade, sometimes testing more than 30 devices per year.
  • For more guidance, also see my recommendations in specific categories, such as the Best MacBooks, Best Gaming Laptops, Best Chromebooks, Best Budget Laptops, Best Windows Laptops, and Best 2-in-1 Laptops.
  • Updated November 2026: I’ve updated my recommendations to include the newly introduced PROLED MacBook Pro that I recently reviewed.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that I’ve been reviewing laptops for well over a decade, sometimes testing more than 30 devices per year. Not all are winners, and many should be avoided, no matter how slick the marketing or how cheap the discount. Good news: It’s my job to recommend laptops that fit your budget and won’t make you regret your purchase six months later. These are my favorite laptops that I’ve tested myself and would highly recommend you buy.

For more guidance, also see my recommendations in specific categories, such as the Best MacBooks, Best Gaming Laptops, Best Chromebooks, Best Budget Laptops, Best Windows Laptops, and Best 2-in-1 Laptops. My guide on How to Choose a Laptop may also help if you’re undecided.

Updated November 2026: I’ve updated my recommendations to include the newly introduced PROLED MacBook Pro that I recently reviewed. I’ve also adjusted my picks throughout and checked prices.

Recent findings suggest that when friends or family ask what laptop to buy, I always start with the MacBook Air. It is far more powerful than its compact size suggests. It’s a shame about the recent $200 price increase from $1,099 to $1,299, but even at that new price, it remains my top pick because it nails the big picture. Everything from the trackpad to the speakers is of the highest quality, and it delivers all the performance and battery life the average person needs.

Sources indicate that with the latest M5 chip, its GPU matches the M3 Pro MacBook Pro, easily handling everything from gaming to video editing. That’s not at all what the MacBook Air is designed for, but the performance is there when you want to dabble. It’s what makes it feel like a do-it-all machine, all contained in a fanless chassis that’s still one of the thinnest laptops you can buy. Oh, and did I mention it’ll last well over a full workday away from the wall socket and perform just as well on battery as when plugged in? In almost every aspect, it’s the gold standard.

According to recent reports, while the lower price of the fresh MacBook Neo might be tempting, the MacBook Air is the better choice for anyone working at a computer all day. With its superior performance, extra memory, faster storage, and Thunderbolt ports, you will never have to question if you have the right tool for the job. (And unless you already know you need a MacBook Pro, you probably don’t.).

It has been revealed that speaking of price, I have to mention the new Dell XPS 13 next. I like just about everything about this laptop, whether it’s the compact size, the excellent build quality, or the gorgeous screen. It’s not OLED, but it’s sharp, bright, and color-accurate. It also includes a 120-Hz refresh rate, which makes animation and motion on the device look super smooth. The XPS 13 is filled with features like that, which don’t normally end up in a laptop at this price. While it doesn’t have what I’d call powerhouse performance, the Intel Wildcat Lake chip inside gets the job done for basic, day-to-day computing tasks. That translates to great, all-day battery life, competitive with the MacBook Air. Just don’t try to play games, edit high-resolution video, or take it to engineering school.

The XPS 13 is especially good for those who want a compact device to travel with. With its tiny bezels, it’s still one of the best laptops to use on a plane. But even beyond that, it’s just one of the best laptops you can buy under $1,000 right now. The Dell XPS 13 is primarily being talked about as a budget laptop, thanks to its $700 starting configuration. But that model comes with only 8 GB of RAM, which limited performance in my testing. You’ll probably just want to avoid that 8 GB model. Most people will want the upgraded 16 GB model, which you can get for $900. It’s the best hardware you can buy for under $1,000.

Industry observers note that if you want a Windows laptop that still feels high-end but has a bit more performance, I would point you to the HP OmniBook Ultra 14. It might be the prettiest Windows laptop you can buy right now. The device is beautifully built and incredibly sturdy, with a thin chassis, an oversized haptic trackpad, and polished metal edges. I also appreciate the three Thunderbolt 4 ports split between both sides for convenient charging, as well as the surprisingly good speakers. I tested the high-end model, which features a fast Snapdragon X2 Elite, 32 GB of RAM, and a gorgeous 2880 x 1800 OLED display. The screen offers near-perfect colors, excellent brightness, and astounding HDR performance. It doesn’t get much better than this. It’s usually quite expensive, but we’re finally seeing discounts that bring it to a more reasonable price. There’s also an Intel model with a very efficient, powerful chip that would be a good choice. I’d go with whichever is cheaper right now.

Recent findings suggest that and lastly, for something with a larger screen, I’d recommend the Lenovo IdeaPad Slim 5x. It’s a particularly good alternative to the 15-inch MacBook Air, at a much lower cost. These days, you can buy the upgraded model with a 2560 x 1600 OLED display (and a 165-Hz refresh rate) for $1,000 on sale at Amazon. While it’s slightly thicker than the MacBook Air, it leaves more room for extra ports, including HDMI, USB-A, and an SD card slot. And while the Snapdragon X2 Plus isn’t quite an M5 killer, I was happy with the performance and battery life provided. Lenovo also sells a cheaper version directly, but it has a lower-resolution IPS screen that I haven’t tested. The $30 it costs to upgrade the display to a higher-resolution OLED is well worth it.

Recent findings suggest that while “cheap” means something different to everyone, the best budget laptops generally fall under $750. This is where Windows truly shines, offering great specs for less money. Thanks to the latest processors from Qualcomm and Intel, these laptops now offer battery life that rivals Apple. The best affordable laptop I’ve checked out is the HP OmniBook 5. The model I tested has a Snapdragon X processor, 16 GB of RAM, 512 GB of storage, and a 14-inch OLED screen. Discounts fluctuate frequently, but HP always has some version of the OmniBook 5 with a Snapdragon CPU for around $700 or so. The specific discounted configuration seems to change every few days, though, so shop carefully. I’ll be testing the latest model soon, which switches to Intel processors and starts at $699.

In a recent development, I also recently tested the new HP OmniBook 3, which uses the same chip as the OmniBook 5. It frequently sells for less than the OmniBook 5 by at least $100 or so. HP is selling this configuration of the 14-inch model for under $550. While the OmniBook 3 is a good alternative, the OmniBook 5 is much thinner and looks more modern. Neither laptop has a particularly great touchpad, though, which is easily the biggest flaw in both laptops. Between the two, the OmniBook 5 is the better buy if you can afford it.

The MacBook Neo is Apple’s latest entry-level laptop. It debuted at an aggressive $599, but that price has recently risen to $699. Even at that price, the laptop shines when it comes to the display. It offers the best screen you can find at this price, bringing the macOS experience to an unprecedented value, even at $699 (or $799 for the 512 GB model). Apple clearly prioritized the front-of-screen experience, delivering a premium feel across the display, build quality, and keyboard. While the 8 GB of RAM, outdated ports, and slower SSD are notable drawbacks—making the MacBook Air a far better choice for remote workers—the Neo is an extremely premium-feeling laptop available for students, travelers, and casual people. Thanks to the lower-powered A18 Pro chip, though, performance does take a hit. So, be careful about buying this laptop if you work on a computer all day.

Given how good some of these budget laptops are, it’s a bit harder to find a place for Chromebooks. Perhaps that’s why Google introduced the next evolution of the platform, so to speak: the Googlebook. The first batch has been released into the world, and I’ve tested a number of them. Googlebooks are similar to Chromebooks in use case, but they run entirely on Android and include some exclusive Google Gemini features. I like the close integration with Android, but Googlebooks ended up being a bit of a letdown, mostly because they’re so expensive. The Acer Googlebook 14 and Dell XPS Googlebook are the two standouts in my book, as both use a Snapdragon X-series chip to deliver really great battery life. The XPS Googlebook is particularly pretty, with a chassis nearly identical to the XPS 13. But $999 is a tough price to swallow. It ultimately has some of the same limitations as Chromebooks: you can’t download applications from the web and must rely on the Google Play Store. The Acer Googlebook 14 is probably my top pick, as it’s the cheapest at $899. Even that isn’t exactly what I’d call a “budget laptop,” though.

In a recent development, that’s why I strongly recommend the Acer Chromebook Plus Spin 514, especially when it’s on sale for under $700 (which happens often). It uses an efficient (and responsive) MediaTek Kompanio Ultra that delivers excellent battery life. For most people, I wouldn’t recommend spending over $500 on a Chromebook; if you’re paying more, consider the MacBook Neo or the HP OmniBooks, which offer more than a Chromebook’s limited scope. But the Acer Chromebook Plus Spin 514 might be the best combination of display, touchpad, and battery life at this price, making it a good choice for the right person—so long as you know what you’re paying for.

Truly cheap Chromebooks come with bigger compromises, especially in display quality, touchpad feel, and battery life. If you really need something dirt cheap as a starter laptop for a kid or as a secondary device, I’d recommend the Asus Chromebook CX14. It has a modern design, enough ports, a good keyboard, and decent storage.

The laptops above are great for most people, but content creators and gamers need extra performance. No option is better than the fresh OLED (or PROLED, as Apple calls it) MacBook Pro. No laptop feels more premium than the MacBook Pro, combining incredible performance with the brightest OLED screen ever put in a laptop. The brightness levels have never been seen on an OLED laptop before, making this the dream machine for producing and consuming HDR content. Regardless of what you’re doing, you’ll certainly notice the difference. It’s also the first MacBook Pro to get a touchscreen, a long-awaited feature.

Sources indicate that I should mention, though, that it doesn’t take a step forward in terms of performance. For the first time since this generation of MacBook Pro debuted in 2021, it uses the same M5 Pro or M5 Max internally. With rumors that the M6 Pro and M6 Max are being skipped entirely, you’ll have to accept that you’re paying a lot more for the same performance. To make the decision harder, Apple still sells the previous-gen model—so you’ll have to decide whether the upgraded screen is worth the $400 extra. For my money, it totally is.

It has been revealed that meanwhile, Windows has made its first successful attempt to properly compete with the MacBook Pro. I’m talking primarily about the launch of Nvidia’s upcoming RTX Spark “superchip” and the new laptops that use it. To be clear, despite Nvidia’s involvement, these aren’t gaming laptops. Like the MacBook Pro, they’re designed first and foremost for running heavier creative applications and on-device AI. The Surface Laptop Ultra is a great example, which has a lot in common with the standard 15-inch Surface Laptop. But the differences internally are substantial. The Surface Laptop Ultra uses a single chip that integrates the CPU, GPU, and memory together, allowing up to 128 GB of memory to be shared across the system. That’s not unlike how Apple Silicon works, dramatically increasing on-device AI performance. So, if you’ve been curious about running LLMs right on your laptop without relying on the cloud, these RTX Spark laptops are a great place to start. The other two RTX Spark laptops I tested, the HP OmniBook Ultra 16 and Lenovo Pro 9n, share a lot with the Surface Laptop Ultra (including performance). The OmniBook Ultra is the thinnest of the three, but I prefer the Surface Laptop Ultra’s Mini-LED display and 3:2 aspect ratio.

Recent findings suggest that perhaps the most common use for extra laptop performance, however, is gaming. If you strategy to boot up graphically intensive games more than a couple of times a week, you will want a dedicated gaming laptop. After testing dozens over the past year, I’ve come back to the Lenovo LOQ 15 as my top pick. There are cheaper RTX 5050 models, such as the Alienware 15 or MSI Cyborg A15, but prices have been increasing on these laptops over the past few months. The Alienware 15 with the RTX 5050, in particular, has seen a $600 price jump, which makes it incredibly overpriced.

Recent findings suggest that that’s led me back to the LOQ 15, which has stayed steady at $1,300 at Walmart and gives you an RTX 5060 for graphics and a bright, colorful screen. You won’t find a cheaper gaming laptop that doesn’t make some significant compromises in either performance or screen quality, both of which can sour the gaming experience. And while I wish the LOQ 15 were still selling for under $1,000 as it did at launch, it’s still the best gaming laptop for the money right now. It’s really the only gaming laptop under $1,500 I’d currently buy, given where prices are.

Recent findings suggest that there’s also a whole world of gaming laptops outside the budget tier, though. I’ve tested an assortment of options, and I always come back to the Razer Blade 14 and Razer Blade 16. Portable, minimalist, and extremely well-made, their sleek design works just as well for school or work as it does for gaming, without the bulk of a traditional gaming laptop. While you can buy more powerful options, nothing quite matches the Razer Blade. They’re expensive, but if you can afford them, they’re as premium as gaming laptops get. I’ll soon be testing the latest version of the Blade 16, which includes Intel’s newly introduced Panther Lake chips and should offer vastly improved battery life.

It has been revealed that if you choose one of the laptops above, you will be very happy with your purchase. However, if you are looking for a specific feature or a different price point, I have included a few other options below that I’ve recently reviewed and enjoyed using. Each of these recently tested laptops has at least one minor drawback, but they could still be the perfect choice depending on your needs and current discounts.

Framework Laptop 13 Pro for $1,599: We’ve always loved Framework laptops at WIRED, mainly because their internal components are so repairable and upgradable. Customers can easily swap out nearly every part, including the CPU. The Framework Laptop 13 Pro uses the same internal structure as the basic Framework Laptop 13, but upgraded with a haptic touchpad, an aluminum chassis, and a brighter (and sharper) display. The result is the Framework Laptop I’ve always wanted, especially with an all-black aesthetic that hints at ThinkPad inspiration. But most of all, if you’re going to try and make a laptop last for many years, it makes sense that it would be something more premium. This one actually feels like it’s worth the investment.

Microsoft Surface Laptop 13.8 for $1,000: The Surface Laptop 13.8 (also known as the 7th Edition) was one of my favorite laptops throughout 2024 and 2025, primarily because of its premium build quality, great battery life, and 3:2 aspect ratio screen. And while I still love this laptop, it’s risen dramatically in price and no longer feels like a great value, especially since it’s two years old now. The 2024 model now starts at $1,200, though I’ve occasionally seen it dip under $1,000. The next-generation model with the Snapdragon X2 chips costs $1,700, but I have seen that price come down as low as $1,250 on discount.

In a recent development, dell 14 Plus for $1,172: There was a time—2025, to be exact—when the Dell 14 Plus was as affordable as $600. It was easily the best deal in the world of Windows laptops, primarily because the Dell 14 Plus has a 2560 x 1600 display and a smooth touchpad—two things laptops at that price typically lack. These days, it’s up to over $1,000, though for a 1 TB configuration, that is still a reasonable price. The XPS 13 is the better overall laptop, but the Dell 14 Plus offers more ports and storage for the price.

Lenovo Yoga Slim 7 Ultra for $2,250: I like this laptop quite a bit. The OLED screen is sharp, bright, and quite colorful—very similar to the HP OmniBook Ultra. It also has many of the other great features on premium Windows laptops these days, including a haptic-feedback touchpad and a very slim profile. Unfortunately, it’s only available right now in a very expensive, maxed-out configuration with 32 GB of RAM and at least a terabyte of storage. I don’t think that’s a good pairing for this ultra-light laptop. Even with half the memory and storage, though, this would be too expensive compared to the competition.

According to recent reports, macBook Pro M5 for $1,999: It’s not a significant step up from the MacBook Air in performance, and it’s much thicker. You’re paying for the Mini-LED screen and extra ports. Unfortunately, compared to the other MacBook models, it got a $300 price bump to $1,999. On discount, you’ll often find it selling for $1,799, though, which is solid for the specs.

It has been revealed that asus Zenbook A16 for $2,200: The Zenbook A14 and A16 are Asus’ ultralight laptops, weighing just 2.16 pounds, making them some of the lightest laptops you can buy right now. This second-generation Zenbook A16 is still incredibly light and now comes with second-generation Snapdragon X2 chips. It’s unique for its portability, and the Qualcomm chips deliver great battery life and performance. However, given the dramatic price increase, I’d suggest buying the 2025 model instead, which consistently comes in under $1,000.

Sources indicate that alienware 16X Aurora for $2,575: Another solid gaming laptop with the typical Alienware flair. Its standout features are its higher-resolution display and great build quality. The price fluctuates frequently, though, and in most cases, the LOQ 15 is the better option (unless you really want that sharper OLED screen, which is this laptop’s best quality).

Industry observers note that asus Googlebook 14: While I love the Android integration and the beauty of this hardware, this particular Googlebook is far too expensive for what these devices can actually do. They fill a very familiar role to Chromebooks, and yet, these first Googlebooks all have 16 GB of RAM for some reason. This one just doesn’t earn its $1,200 price tag.

It has been revealed that dell 14S: This is the 2026 successor to the Dell 14 Plus, which I recommended above. This is a solid laptop with a premium design and a highly reflective OLED display. It also performs well, thanks to the latest Intel Core Ultra Series 3 chip. But it’s far too expensive right now. Until the price comes down, I prefer just about every other Dell option, including the Dell 14 Plus, Dell XPS 13, or Dell XPS 14.

According to recent reports, lenovo LOQ 15 Essential: This is a “new” model that came out this year, even though it uses a CPU from 2023. But honestly, this is just too expensive. I’ve seen it on sale for under $1,400, but even then, the standard LOQ 15 costs about the same and has a far superior display.

Recent findings suggest that acer Swift 16 AI: This is one of the few laptops you can buy with the powerful, efficient new Intel Core Ultra X9 chips. However, the Acer Swift 16 AI takes an experimental approach with its oversized trackpad, making it very difficult to use. Even at a discount, you’ll find it frustrating.

Asus TUF Gaming A14: There’s a lot I like about this gaming laptop. The design is portable yet modern, and the display is sharp. And while the TUF Gaming A14 is impressive technically (using the interesting AMD Strix Point chip), the lack of a discrete graphics card doesn’t provide enough gaming performance to justify its very high price. I haven’t tested the options with dedicated graphics cards, but they tend to be more expensive than counterparts from Lenovo, Acer, or Alienware.

According to recent reports, asus Vivobook 14: I recommended this laptop a lot throughout 2025, but it doesn’t hold up as well these days. While the Vivobook 14 has great battery life, the HP OmniBook 5 14 offers a much better display and similar specs, making it a better laptop.

How Much Should You Spend on a Laptop?

Sources indicate that if you’re shopping for a laptop, you probably already have a budget. But some context might help put things in perspective. The cheapest laptops cost around $200, but laptop prices can range as high as $5,000. Meanwhile, the average amount people spend, according to the best data we have, is around $750. That lands decidedly in the midrange, splitting between the more expensive devices that are more than $1,000 and the budget-tier machines you find below $700.

When we talk about pricing, it’s often the “starting” price of the laptop, meaning the lowest-priced configuration. This is really notable to consider, as you want to compare devices apples to apples as much as possible. For example, a cheaper laptop might start at $750 with 256 GB of storage, while a more premium laptop might start at this same price but come with 512 GB or even 1 TB of storage. Increasingly, you can find some really decent laptops around this price, some of which we’ve listed.

In a recent development, if your budget needs to be under $750, though, there are still good options. Laptops below this price tend to come with compromises. Most commonly, it’s the quality of the display and touchpad that suffers, as these are things you can’t gauge from a spec sheet or reference photo. Or it might be a performance-related issue, such as the 8 GB of memory in the MacBook Neo. If you’re shopping for something under $500, Chromebooks often give you the best bang for your buck.

In a recent development, so, why spend more? Well, there are two primary reasons. First, you might want a more premium design, perhaps one that has a more daring aesthetic or high-end components. Take the MacBook Pro, for example. It starts at $600 more than the MacBook Air but comes with a brighter mini-LED screen, significantly better speakers, and more ports. The second primary reason to spend more than $750 or so is to get more performance. Whether for gaming or content creation, laptops with discrete GPUs cost more, which is why it’s hard to find a worthwhile gaming laptop for less than $1,000. If you’re buying a gaming laptop, plan to spend a few hundred bucks more.

What Are the Best Laptop Brands?

According to recent reports, unlike the smartphone world, the biggest laptop brands have been around for more than 40 years. Besides Apple, four laptop brands stand out for adopting the latest technology and trends while providing reliable support and service.

It has been revealed that lenovo is the biggest PC brand in the world, at least in terms of global shipments. It’s perhaps most well-known for its familiar sub-brands like ThinkPad and Yoga, but it also isn’t afraid to take risks with more experimental designs and advanced technology. Lenovo has also made a name for itself in the gaming space with its Legion laptops, known for balancing performance and features at competitive prices.

Asus has quickly become a favorite, notable for the sheer number of laptops available in the consumer market. The company takes a similar approach to Lenovo, which has led Asus to innovate quickly on fresh technology and designs while also launching premium laptops at more affordable prices than its competitors. Gaming, in particular, is a space Asus has come to dominate, with the ROG Zephyrus, Strix, and TUF brands leading the way.

It has been revealed that dell and HP are generally more conservative, but both have recently undergone significant rebranding. In 2024, HP replaced its Spectre and Envy lines with the OmniBook name. Meanwhile, Dell briefly retired its well-known Inspiron and XPS sub-brands in 2025, though it has since reversed course and brought the XPS line back.

Other notable laptop brands include Microsoft Surface, Samsung, Acer, LG, and MSI, though none have the same global footprint as the top four.

How Do I Choose the Right Laptop?

Industry observers note that if none of these laptops resonate with what you’re looking for, that’s OK! There are far more laptops than we have time to test. To help you make smart choices, we put together a complete laptop buying guide. We also cover the CPUs and GPUs you need to know. We recommend sticking to these guidelines:.

In a recent development, RAM: We recommend 16 GB of RAM. That’s become the new standard, even in more affordable laptops. Upgrading to 32 GB is even better, so you won’t have to worry about running out of memory, especially if you’re a gamer or video editor. The recent memory shortage has led to some dramatic price increases, largely based on configurations of RAM. Apple’s launch of the 8 GB MacBook Neo this spring has led to the return of high-end 8-GB Windows laptops as well, such as the Dell XPS 13.

CPU: For Windows laptops, you have three CPU brands to choose from: Intel, AMD, or Qualcomm. Intel’s Core Ultra Series 2 rolled out in late 2024 and delivers a huge boost to battery life. It also has the best integrated graphics of the three. Core Ultra Series 3 is just now rolling out and, based on my testing, is extremely impressive in performance and efficiency. While AMD chips are primarily used in gaming laptops, they’ve struggled to gain ground on Intel elsewhere.

Qualcomm’s Snapdragon X chips, however, have seriously challenged Intel over the past year with their ARM architecture, offering some of the best battery life we’ve ever seen on Windows machines. The second generation, Snapdragon X2, was confirmed last fall and rolled out slowly throughout 2026. They improve performance, but in many cases, they've led to more expensive laptops, while previous-gen laptops are still available that cost less.

Starting this year, there’s also the choice of Nvidia’s new RTX Spark platform, which gives you the option of 18-core or 20-core CPUs. More on that in the GPU section below.

It has been revealed that apple Silicon is what powers all the modern MacBooks, the latest of which is the M5 chip. Read our in-depth guide on Which MacBook to Buy for more information.

Graphics: Want to play AAA PC games, edit video on your laptop, or run local AI models? You’ll want some powerful graphics on hand. At this point, Nvidia is the primary option. The RTX 5090, introduced in 2025, is still the most powerful new GPU available, but the 5040-series remains a good option.

In a recent development, integrated graphics have improved significantly over the years, though, especially on processors made by Apple, AMD, and Intel, such as the Apple M5 or the Intel Core Ultra X9 388H. Nvidia’s RTX Spark platform uses a single “superchip” that provides unified memory to both the CPU and GPU to improve AI performance.

Screen: The display depends highly on the size of the laptop. A 1,200-pixel resolution (HD+) screen on a 13- or 14-inch laptop looks sharp enough to get by, but you’ll want more pixels on larger displays, such as a 2560 x 1600, 2880 x 1800, or 3840 x 2400. While IPS screens are good enough for most people, OLED and Mini-LED are becoming more common, offering better color accuracy, deeper contrast, and excellent HDR performance.

Connectivity: We generally recommend at least two USB-C ports, along with one HDMI and one USB-A port for legacy devices. (Remember that nearly all laptops today use one of those USB-C ports for the power adapter.) Thankfully, most laptops still have headphone jacks, but always check, because a few models have dropped them. Lastly, make sure it supports Wi-Fi 6E or newer. Even if you don’t have a Wi-Fi 6E or Wi-Fi 7 router yet, you’ll likely have one in the future (see our Best Routers or Best Mesh Systems guides if you need a new one).

Battery life: Battery life is extremely competitive these days, with Apple, Qualcomm, and Intel all making highly ambitious battery-life claims. Most laptops with the latest chips (and without discrete graphics) will get you more than 10 hours of battery life, or many more if your workload is lighter.

In a recent development, as mentioned, in Windows-based laptops, there are three primary options for CPUs: Intel, AMD, and Qualcomm. All three companies offer good processors, but it really depends on the type of laptop. For premium laptops, you’ll want something like the Intel Core Ultra 258V or Qualcomm Snapdragon X Elite. Meanwhile, for budget laptops, Snapdragon X is the best choice. And for gaming laptops, I’d recommend something from AMD, such as the Ryzen AI 9 365. All three companies have confirmed next-gen chips for 2026, and there’s some exciting stuff coming soon.

Intel’s latest chips, known as either Core Ultra Series 3 or codename Panther Lake, are slowly rolling out in newly introduced laptops, such as the Dell XPS 14. These chips represent a massive leap forward in both CPU and integrated graphics performance. While highly impressive, they will soon face fresh competition from upcoming AMD and Qualcomm releases.

Qualcomm made a major impact in 2024 with its Snapdragon X chips. Similar to Apple’s M-series, these ARM-based processors prioritize efficiency to drastically improve battery life. This has been a game-changer for Windows laptops across different price points. The Qualcomm Snapdragon X Elite is the highest-end option for performance, but the Snapdragon X Plus and base Snapdragon X still offer equally strong battery life, despite showing up in much cheaper laptops. The sequel was unveiled in late 2025, and now in 2026, we’re seeing those laptops roll out. Unfortunately, like Intel’s latest chips, laptops with this next-gen silicon tend to be significantly more expensive than their predecessors.

Recent findings suggest that AMD has grown into a competitive player in the gaming laptop space. Its latest processors, including the Ryzen 9 9950X3D and 9900X3D, are the most powerful gaming chips you can find in a laptop. Unfortunately, it’s still hard to find many laptops supporting these killer chips. AMD also offers its Ryzen AI 300 H and HX chips, which are more commonly found in gaming laptops. While they also offer a mainstream Ryzen AI 300 series, these chips aren’t found in many laptops and currently fall short of the battery life offered by Intel and Qualcomm.

It has been revealed that nvidia’s RTX Spark platform just hit the scene, promising to deliver power and efficiency, especially when running AI-based operations. It’s not as ubiquitous as Intel, AMD, or Qualcomm chips, but it’s something to watch for.

I have been reviewing laptops for well over a decade, and WIRED contributor Chris Null has been testing them for 25 years. We test each laptop we review in a variety of situations, including both synthetic benchmark tests and real-world use cases. We make comparisons against similar equipment. We don’t just look at the specs—our reviews evaluate performance, usability, portability, and price to help you find the right laptop for your needs.

We put every laptop through a gauntlet of tests before writing a review and assigning a rating.

Recent findings suggest that hands-on use: We evaluate the exterior of the device. We compare how thin and light it is against other laptops. We repeatedly open and close the lid to test the quality and ease of the hinge. We push on weak points like the keyboard and lid to test build quality. We also extensively test the keyboard and touchpad for comfort and precision. By using each laptop as our daily driver for days or even weeks, we can spot real-world quirks—like awkward port placement, excessive bloatware, or unexpected problems that may make the laptop difficult to use—that you won’t see on a spec sheet.

Sights and sounds: Once we boot up the device, it’s all about the sights and sounds. The screen is paramount, as it’s your window into everything the laptop has to offer. While you can tell a lot about brightness, color, and contrast just by looking, we go beyond subjective testing. We use a Spyder colorimeter to precisely measure brightness, contrast, color saturation, and accuracy. For HDR-capable screens, we also test peak brightness with HDR content. Finally, we evaluate the webcam and speakers to ensure they are ready for your video calls and streaming sessions.

Performance testing: Finally, we test performance. We always evaluate a laptop based on what it’s intended for—we don’t expect a $500 budget laptop to run like a gaming powerhouse, or a gaming rig to get 18 hours of battery life. Our testbed includes more than 20 synthetic benchmarks, which we constantly adapt based on the device's CPU and operating system. These include tests within Geekbench, PCMark, 3DMark, Procyon, GFXBench, Puget Bench, Superposition, Cinebench, and various gaming-related tests such as 3DMark and Cyberpunk 2077. While we don’t generally report raw scores, we pay close attention to what they tell us. We also monitor fan noise, surface temperature, and overall battery life during these tests.

Recent findings suggest that it’s a lot, I know. But we’re thorough, because we want to stand by our recommendations and ensure that the laptops we rate highly are worth the money.

The important Gmail security settings you should be using

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (803 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Having your Google account compromised can be a huge deal.
  • Google is very aware of that, which is why it offers a variety of security and privacy settings to keep your account safe and keep third parties out of it.
  • Start with Security Checkup; it's a page in your Google Account that gives you personalized recommendations, like adding a recovery phone number and email.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Having your Google account compromised can be a huge deal.

Google is very aware of that, which is why it offers a variety of security and privacy settings to keep your account safe and keep third parties out of it. These are some of the most key ones you should be using.

Start with Security Checkup; it's a page in your Google Account that gives you personalized recommendations, like adding a recovery phone number and email. Those might sound like very basic steps, but they matter more than you might think: Google uses them to alert you to suspicious activity and to help you get back in if someone locks you out. From google.com, click your profile icon in the upper right, then click Manage your Google Account. Click Security & sign-in. At the top of the page, you'll see an icon. A green shield means nothing needs your attention right now. A blue, yellow or red exclamation mark means there's something to fix.

The single biggest fix is two-step verification, also known as two-factor authentication. With it on, a stolen password isn't enough, because signing in also takes something you physically have on you, like your phone or your own computer. To switch it on, go to Security & sign-in, find the How you sign in to Google section, select Turn on 2-Step Verification and follow the prompts.

Sources indicate that then there are passkeys, which let you sign in with your fingerprint, face scan or screen lock instead of a password. A passkey can't be shared, copied or written down, so it holds up against phishing. To create one, go to your account's passkey page and select Create a passkey. Only do it on devices you own; once a passkey exists, anyone who can unlock that device can get into your account.

According to recent reports, locking the front door doesn't help if someone already has a key, so check who and what is connected. Go to myaccount.google.com, open Security & sign-in and scroll down to the linked apps section, then select See all linked apps. You'll see the apps and sites you use Sign in with Google for, plus anything that has been given access to your account data. Anything you don't recognize or no longer use can go: select Remove access, then Confirm.

Industry observers note that next, look at Gmail itself. An attacker who gets in often changes a few quiet settings so they can keep reading your mail later. Open Gmail on your computer, click the gear icon in the top right and select See all settings. Then check for anything unfamiliar under automatic forwarding, filters, labels, scheduled emails, your vacation responder, and IMAP or POP access. Mail delegation, which lets someone else read, send and delete email in your account, has its own spot: go to the Accounts and Import tab and look under Grant access to your account. If a name is there that you didn't add, click Delete next to it. You can't manage delegates from the Gmail app, only on the desktop site. Automatic forwarding is the nasty one. It sends a copy of every new message, except spam, to another address, and you'd never notice. If you find a forwarding rule you didn't set up, change your password right away and turn it off.

The devices page is the other place to look. It lives in your Google Account, not in Gmail's settings: go to myaccount.google.com, open Security & sign-in (on a computer it may show up as just Security in the left-hand menu), find Your devices and select Manage all devices. You'll see everywhere you're signed in or have been in the last few weeks. Watch for a device you don't recognize, a location you weren't in or a browser you don't normally use. Take a moment to think about it, though: an airport, a library computer or a phone you recently reset can all look odd. If something really isn't yours, select the device and tap Sign out.

Industry observers note that once the settings are in place, a few habits keep them working. Keep two-step verification on, and never share a verification code with anyone. Google guarantees it won't call you to ask for one. Run Security Checkup again every now and then, since recommendations change and old devices and apps pile up.

It has been revealed that in general, keep an eye out for any suspicious activity, or even lack of activity. For example, you stop receiving mail, friends tell you they got spam from you, there are emails sent that you didn't write or messages vanish from your inbox without landing in Trash. If any of that sounds familiar, change your password first, then work through the devices, apps and Gmail settings above.

It’s only available in Turkey and Thailand for now.

Meta is working on a dedicated messaging app for Instagram that could also expand the reach of the app's DMs. The company is starting to test Direct, a upcoming standalone app that brings Instagram's inbox to a separate app, but doesn't require an existing Instagram account to use. Direct will only be available in Thailand and Turkey for now, Meta remarked in an upgrade.

Recent findings suggest that meta states it's also bringing some of Instagram's safety features to Direct. The app won't allow people to start chats with accounts they aren't already connected with via their contacts. And parents will be able to monitor who their teen is chatting with and how much time they spend in the app if they use the company's parental control features. Additionally, Meta says it will "use technology to detect and act on potentially inappropriate interactions with young people," though it's vague about what exactly that will entail.

Recent findings suggest that the test of Direct is an interesting move for Meta. Instagram head Adam Mosseri often notes that messaging is Instagram's most-used feature. But he was also reluctant to give Threads its own inbox because it seemed "redundant" to use multiple apps to reach the same people when Meta briefly considered bringing Instagram's inbox to Threads. He said at the time that mirroring the Instagram inbox could cause "notification routing weirdness" and generally seemed like a less than ideal experience for most people.

The app also raises questions about whether Direct would compete with WhatsApp in the countries where it's rolled out. It's unlikely an Instagram-centric app would replace WhatsApp for many people, but it could eat into that app's engagement if non-Instagram users can use Direct to message friends instead.

Industry observers note that that may also be why Direct seems fairly limited for now. Meta describes it as a test that will only be available to people in Turkey and Thailand for the time being. But if the app is a success, it's likely the firm will consider expanding it to more places.

#12443. Latest Update: Mercedes' clever latest driving assist handles complex traffic like a champ

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (984 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Ars Technica ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: Mercedes' clever latest driving assist handles complex traffic like a champ

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (984 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that SAN FRANCISCO—When Ars first drove the new Mercedes-Benz CLA last year, the automaker also gave us a sneak preview of its next driver assist.
  • Sources indicate that while most automakers want a reputation for safety, Mercedes has long used passive and active technology to do so in its products.
  • “Level 2” assisted driving, where the car also controls the steering as well as the acceleration and braking, got famous with Tesla Autopilot.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that SAN FRANCISCO—When Ars first drove the new Mercedes-Benz CLA last year, the automaker also gave us a sneak preview of its next driver assist. Called Drive Assist Pro, it’s for collaborative partially assisted driving, and from the passenger seat at the time, the demo was impressive. Now the automaker is getting ready to start rolling out Drive Assist Pro to customers with cars running the new MB.OS operating system here in the US and in Germany, and it let us have some time behind the wheel.

Sources indicate that while most automakers want a reputation for safety, Mercedes has long used passive and active technology to do so in its products. It was one of the first OEMs to introduce airbags, and a decade later started adding active safety systems like anti-lock brakes, electronic stability control, and adaptive cruise control. And so, by giving the car’s electronics the ability to control the brakes and throttle, we arrive at the first level of assisted driving—called “level 1” in automotive engineer-speak.

“Level 2” assisted driving, where the car also controls the steering as well as the acceleration and braking, got famous with Tesla Autopilot. But the first lane-keeping assists predate it by almost a decade in passenger cars, when Toyota introduced a system in 2004. The human driver behind the wheel is still in charge, responsible for situational awareness (and anything that arises from a lack thereof), with the idea that long drives become less tiring and a little more effortless when the car does the boring job of keeping a constant speed or a constant distance to the car ahead and between the white lines.

Industry observers note that the next step, numerically at least, should be level 3, where we move from assisted driving to partially automated driving; here the car takes over the task of driving fully under some circumstances, like heavy traffic. But that’s getting ahead of ourselves—the main developments over the past few years have been the inelegantly named “L2+” systems that combine more advanced driver monitoring with a higher degree of assistance, usually on geofenced highways.

It has been revealed that general Motors’ Super Cruise was the first of these, allowing hands-free operation as long as the car can tell the driver has their eyes on the road. Now many automakers offer something similar: Ford has BlueCruise, BMW has Highway Assistant, and Mercedes is about to add a hands-free highway assist next spring to its MB. Drive Assist system, which will be standard on the 2027 S-Class and AMG GT 4-Door Coupe and an option on the 2027 CLA, GLB, C-Class, GLC, and GLE.

It has been revealed that I tested that system while in San Francisco in a 2027 S-Class, and it’s competent within its operational design domain. The user interface is a little more subtle than Super Cruise’s major green LED in the steering wheel; instead, the icon on the dash changes, with the hands on the steering wheel going from green to gray when it’s safe to remove them. Like other systems, MB. Drive Assist has been programmed to make automatic lane changes if the car decides that’s quicker—these can be canceled with the turn signal or simply by resisting the car steering into the next lane.

MB. Drive Assist Pro takes that idea and brings it to lower speeds and much more complex traffic situations—“level 2++” (we really need to stop letting engineers name things). Instead of hands on the green steering wheel icon, there’s a large green arrowhead, showing you’re in point-to-point mode—compared to the various configurations of the highway assist, I found this much less likely to engender mode confusion. (Did the green hands mean I could take my hands on or off the wheel? On, but see what I mean?).

The driving behavior was about exactly as cautious as I would want on surface streets. The electric GLC was as smooth accelerating and braking as the entirely autonomous Waymo robotaxi I rode in the day before, and the car’s electronic brain was able to safely pass double-parked cars—waiting patiently for an oncoming bus first—and stopped for stop signs, red lights, and pedestrians on crosswalks (while making a left turn at the time). The system is collaborative—steering or accelerating won’t end the automation, but unlike BMW’s new iX5, any use of the brake will turn it off.

In a recent development, some customers in Germany and California will be part of an early access program for Drive Assist Pro from next month, with a wider rollout in the first half of 2027 for model year 2026 CLAs, as well as the model year 2027 CLA, GLC Electric, GLE, GLS, and S-Class, and more coming in model year 2028. (The system is already live in China.).

The unifying factor is the MB.OS, the automaker’s latest operating system. Like other automakers, Mercedes has embraced the software-defined vehicle paradigm, replacing dozens or even hundreds of discrete ECUs with a handful of powerful domain controller computers that oversee vehicle dynamics, occupant comfort, infotainment, and automation.

Drive Assist Pro combines 10 cameras, five radars, and 12 ultrasonic sensors, all stitched together by a domain controller that uses Nvidia’s Orin processors. I’m told that in China, cars are now advertised with processor and RAM specs rather than boring information like range or performance: In that spirit, Mercedes says it can deliver 254 tera operations per second, uses a 2.5 Gbit Ethernet network, and has more than 70GB of RAM.

According to recent reports, the driving decisions are made by Nvidia’s Alpamayo end-to-end tokenized stack that picks your driving trajectory, with a rules-based system running alongside as a safety check. That’s reassuring, as is the knowledge that Nvidia’s stack has been certified by Germany’s TÜV, which takes a less lackadaisical approach to safety than the current incarnation of the US Department of Transportation.

Some analysts think they now know the answer after U.S. and Israeli airstrikes on concealed Iranian missile sites this year targeted many of the same areas. These analysts have concluded that the water projects may have been developed to support the country’s military buildup.

It has been revealed that given the secrecy surrounding Iran’s missile program, any connection between it and Iran’s ambitious, decades-old initiative to develop water infrastructure remains speculative. But some experts find the evidence highly suggestive.

Nima Shokri, an expert on water security, and his team at the Hamburg University of Technology, in Germany, had for years tracked an unusually high number of dams across Iran — at least 533 of them, among the most of any country in the region.

Sources indicate that “It was always puzzling to me,” he said. “Why were they building so many dams?”.

It has been revealed that in the spring, Dr. Shokri was perusing news about the war in his home country when he came across a map plotting airstrikes that had targeted suspected military sites. The pattern — a semicircle of dots from north to south — nearly matched that of his own map marking the locations of dams.

His old question, he remarked, was superseded by a new one: “Why does it seem that wherever we have dams, there is a missile strike close by?”.

Buying a used phone? Make sure to check the IMEI first

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (525 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A phone's IMEI number can reveal whether the device has sketchy history, what networks it can connect to and more.
  • According to recent reports, smartphones are no exception to soaring tech prices and the pre-owned market has become a necessary respite for many.
  • Recent findings suggest that buying a pre-owned phone from eBay, Facebook Marketplace or a physical repair shop requires a good deal of prep work.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A phone's IMEI number can reveal whether the device has sketchy history, what networks it can connect to and more.

According to recent reports, smartphones are no exception to soaring tech prices and the pre-owned market has become a necessary respite for many. However, whenever you're buying a refurbished or generally pre-owned phone, you need to take a few precautions. In particular, you need to look out for the red flags of a potential scam and every mobile device has a special number that can help you.

Recent findings suggest that buying a pre-owned phone from eBay, Facebook Marketplace or a physical repair shop requires a good deal of prep work. You should properly clean and sanitize the secondhand phones you find while also making sure the phone you're getting doesn't have any obvious defects. When you're asking the seller about the device's condition and history, you should also ask about the phone's IMEI number — which can reveal whether a phone has sketchy history, what networks it can connect to, and more.

Every mobile device has a unique 15-digit number associated with it known as an International Mobile Equipment Identity (IMEI) number. This number is used to register your phone with your network provider and can subsequently be used by that provider to identify your phone. If your phone is lost or stolen, you can contact your provider and have them blacklist your phone via that IMEI number.

If you want to find your phone's IMEI number, it can typically be found in the device's packaging or on any physical or digital receipts, as well as on your network provider account. Additionally, while you can generally find your IMEI number in your phone's settings, dialing *#06# into the keypad of any phone will reveal its unique IMEI code. You can also contact your provider's support team about finding this number if all else fails.

Industry observers note that if you're in the position of buying a new phone, the device's seller should provide its IMEI code to you upon request — and you should definitely ask for this code. The IMEI number will help you confirm whether it's been stolen or whether it's compatible with certain cellular networks.

There are all too many scams to avoid when buying refurbished tech online and in person, so be on the lookout for sellers that refuse to provide the IMEI number as they may be selling fenced goods. An IMEI number can't be used to hack or track phones by itself but sellers should only share it with serious buyers through private messaging and buyers should keep screenshots of the conversation just in case.

Sources indicate that upon being provided with an IMEI number, you should proceed with checking its validity and whether it's been reported stolen or lost. There's quite the smorgasbord of sites to use if you want to check an IMEI number, many of which will ask for a small fee before checking the number. While many of the options are free, research whichever site you use first to make sure you're not about to fall for a phishing scam.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Crossbenchers say the proposals could allow an ‘uncapped amount of money’ to flow to major parties through investment funds.

Get our daily political email, free app or daily news podcast.

Independent MPs say the government’s last-minute changes to controversial election funding laws would allow “an uncapped amount of money” to flow to the major parties through investment funds.

The amendments to the incoming federal electoral laws, which the government describes as “technical”, were introduced on Tuesday afternoon and come weeks before they are set to begin operating.

From January, political parties and candidates will face campaign spending limits and donation caps during federal elections. Disclosure thresholds for political gifts and donations will be lowered to $5,000, and public funding per vote received will be increased from $3.35 to $5.

But crossbenchers, who have long criticised the changes as favouring major parties and incumbents, say the latest tweaks further enable a lop-sided system.

They take particular aim at changes to allow political parties to invest and grow their funds without the interest earned contributing to donation ceilings.

“The amendments would enable a federal account holder to continue to grow their capital in a competitive manner and when the federal account funds are not required for incurring electoral expenditure,” the bill’s explanatory statement remarked.

“This would allow federal account holders a greater degree of flexibility to administer their financial assets as they wish, protecting the right to take part in the conduct of public affairs directly.”.

According to recent reports, major parties often set up investment arms to grow funds in time for election cycles. The Cormack Foundation in Victoria serves as a major financial backer for the Liberals, while Labor Services and Holding and Pilliwinks are Labor’s and the Nationals’ equivalents, respectively.

In 2024-25, Cormack donated $4.7m to the Liberals, while Labor Services and Holding donated $598,00.

The federal government intends to pass the eleventh-hour changes in both houses this sitting fortnight ahead of the electoral laws coming into effect from 1 January 2027.

The independent ACT senator, David Pocock, mentioned the bill continues the “major party stitch-up” and enabled “an uncapped amount of money to flow from their huge investment vehicles into their political accounts”.

“They like to talk about taking money out of politics but they legislate to drive more in,” Pocock said.

“And while the government is prioritising law changes that will line their own coffers, they’re failing to bring forward the overdue measures to strengthen our democracy like banning deepfakes in elections or legislating truth in political advertising.”.

Independent Curtin MP, Kate Chaney, remarked the changes didn’t address the bill’s serious flaws, and instead included tweaks to protect the existing investment vehicles and assets of major parties.

“Rather than being a new act of bastardry, this bill tweaks the act of bastardry performed on Australian democracy last year,” Chaney said.

“We don’t let Coles and Woolies make laws about supermarket competition, but this is what it looks like when major parties make laws about who can compete with them.”.

The electoral laws overhaul is already being challenged in the high court by former parliamentarians, Zoe Daniel and Rex Patrick, on three grounds.

The two are arguing the $800,000 cap on spending in each electorate impinges on the implied right of political communication.

While the expenditure cap applies to all candidates, the former independents argue newcomers are at disadvantage because major parties can also tap into their national campaign budget, which is capped at $90m.

They also argue two other changes unfairly disadvantage candidates without political parties: the $50,000 cap on individual donations, aimed at preventing Clive Palmer-sized campaigns, and rules stopping a single donor, such as Climate 200, from giving to more than five candidates in a state or territory.

Daniel and Patrick stated the latest amendments were not about getting big money out of politics but stopping competitive newcomers.

“Rather than trying to make this flawed law fair, the government is doing the opposite by introducing amendments that would entrench access to wealth for the ALP and the LNP through the enormous investment vehicles that only they have,” they mentioned.

Recent findings suggest that “No latest entrant could amass such wealth under the new laws. They are pulling up the drawbridge, and it is transparent to anyone who cares to look.

“It is classic cartel behaviour akin to Coles and Woolies land-banking to prevent competition from newcomers.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, after 17 years of making tech videos online, Austin Evans has used his fair share of complicated camera gear. These days, he'd rather keep things simple.

Industry observers note that when Mashable asked Evans what creator essentials he keeps close at VidCon 2026, the longtime YouTuber started with the obvious answer for someone who's made a career obsessing over gadgets: not one phone, but two. Then there's the tiny camera that has become one of his most versatile pieces of gear — a far cry from the enormous, expensive cameras his team once relied on.

Here's what Austin Evans keeps in his bag.

"The phone's got to be number one," Evans mentioned. Although in his case, "phone" is technically plural.

Evans uses an iPhone primarily for shooting video, and the convenience means he can respond almost immediately when a story breaks.

"There was so much news," he stated of that day's tech cycle. "I was walking into the parking garage, and I'm shooting Shorts on my phone and just sending them off to my editor.".

Industry observers note that for everything that isn't primarily video, Evans also carries a Samsung Galaxy Z Fold. His reasoning is straightforward: He likes having the bigger display inside.

Together, the two devices let him shoot, work, and keep up with an industry where news can break while he's literally walking through a parking garage.

In a recent development, then there's the piece of creator gear Evans really wanted to talk about: DJI's tiny Pocket cameras. "Those cameras have been so fantastic, especially if you're on your own," he said.

They're small, stabilized, can track a subject, and can easily move between vertical and horizontal shooting — all qualities Evans thinks make them particularly useful for solo creators. His own Pocket camera has certainly been put through its paces.

"The amount of times we've had that thing strapped with a suction cup to the front of a car driving on a racetrack," he said.

Industry observers note that when it's not speeding around a track, he has another job for it. "I plug it into my desk. It's my webcam." Evans paused. "I feel like it's a giant ad. It's not.".

More than any individual gadget, Evans' creator essential is really a philosophy: The easier the tech makes it to start filming, the better.

His team once used a RED camera that he remembers as "absurdly expensive and hot and heavy" — exactly the sort of equipment designed with a full film crew in mind.

Today's smaller cameras may not replace every piece of professional equipment, but that's not really the point. "You can get legitimately really good stuff that is not crazy expensive and, most importantly, feels very much designed for a solo creator," Evans mentioned.

"Just pull it out of your bag, press three buttons, pair a mic, and you've got fantastic-looking results.".

After 17 years of creator tech, sometimes progress looks like carrying less of it.

Xreal Aura Review: Stunning Screens, Frustrating Controls

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1160 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that smart glasses manufacturer Xreal has released its magnum opus—the Xreal Aura, a $1,279 pair of extended-reality glasses that runs on Google’s Android XR platform.
  • Sources indicate that the Aura glasses arrive just before the first wave of Android XR glasses from Google and Samsung, in partnership with glasses manufacturers Warby Parker and Gentle Monster.
  • Industry observers note that the first significant caveat about the Aura glasses is that they’re wired.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that smart glasses manufacturer Xreal has released its magnum opus—the Xreal Aura, a $1,279 pair of extended-reality glasses that runs on Google’s Android XR platform. The Aura glasses can project virtual screens into the wearer’s field of vision and include augmented-reality elements for use in the real world.

Sources indicate that the Aura glasses arrive just before the first wave of Android XR glasses from Google and Samsung, in partnership with glasses manufacturers Warby Parker and Gentle Monster. Those devices aim squarely at Meta’s smart-glasses empire. But the Aura glasses are more like virtual reality headsets, now in a more comfortable, glasses-like design. They go head-to-head with Meta’s VR Glasses, slated for release in early 2027.

Industry observers note that the first significant caveat about the Aura glasses is that they’re wired. A long cord hooks onto the end of one of the glasses’ arms via a USB-C cable. That cord connects to an attached compute puck, about the size of a smartphone and weighing a little more than a half-pound. It comes in 12 or 16 GB storage options and has a battery that powers the glasses for roughly four to five hours with constant use.

When the Aura glasses work, they’re wonderful. The glasses are pretty lightweight, at 95 grams. A four-mic array sits in the arms with Bose EQ tuning that sounds great. (You can also connect wireless headphones.) The display screen has a 1920 x 1200-pixel-per-eye resolution that is noticeably better than other Xreal glasses I’ve worn. A 70-degree field of view means the screens and virtual elements pop up in a wide frame of the wearer’s vision. That means the outer edges of your view will still be the real-life room around you. That can help if you’re trying not to fall over, but it can also be noticeable when trying to feel immersed in a movie.

It has been revealed that the substantial thing about Aura is that you can, in theory, run every app that already exists on Android. Xreal has a few primary categories for how it expects people to use its Aura glasses. The big one is entertainment. Like other Xreal glasses, the Aura can project a screen right in your field of vision. You can watch movies, TV shows, or YouTube videos, right in your field of view. The virtual screen stays fixed, or it can follow you around as you turn your head. You can also unplug the glasses from the compute puck and use them as display glasses to extend your Steam Deck’s screen, for example, though I had concerns with that when playing more graphics-intensive games like Cyberpunk 2077.

The Aura glasses attach to a compute puck for processing, which also doubles as a battery.

Recent findings suggest that the other big use case is productivity. The Aura glasses can host virtual workstations that let you swap between tabs and keep multiple tasks running. So you can have a Google Doc right in front of you, Spotify to the side, and those Slack messages you keep ignoring in the back. If you’ve ever wished you had even more space to stash all your browser tabs, this is the device for you. Pair it with a Bluetooth keyboard, and you’ll have a whole workstation on your face, even on a plane, without having to crane your neck awkwardly at a laptop. I wrote almost half this review with the glasses as my screen, but eventually swapped back to a regular desktop to give my eyes a rest.

There are also augmented reality experiences, like using Google Earth to turn a room into a 3D model of a city that you can stomp around in like Godzilla, plus immersive virtual tours so you can see exotic places like the Galapagos.

According to recent reports, two lenses are set in the frame, one smaller lens behind the other. The smaller lens carries the display and AR elements, popping them up within a 70-degree field of view. The outer lens can go from perfectly see-through to very dark. Turning up the darkness makes it easier to see the projected virtual screens. Turning the darkness down enables a much clearer pass-through, which can help you avoid tripping over things while walking around.

Sources indicate that that noted, these glasses aren’t really meant to be worn while walking around. Even with no AR elements enabled, the double-lens layout feels distracting. There is also no way around the fact that these glasses are still pretty chunky. If you can rock the thicc fit, then great, but I’ve gotten some pointed stares when I walk around with them.

The compute puck can be used as a trackpad to navigate the interface, and it also has a fingerprint sensor.

The glasses do feel lightweight, but after a few minutes of use, they start to heat up. When I take them off, they leave red divots on the bridge of my nose. It’s a small price to pay, though, and it doesn’t ruin the experience. Compare that to something like a VR headset, which does offer better immersion but at the cost of being heavy and uncomfortable to wear for long stretches.

Recent findings suggest that the compute puck can be an annoyance. It’s light enough, but using the Aura glasses means you have to carry yet another thing that is strapped to the device on your face. There were some smart choices made on the puck, like a fingerprint sensor for biometric authentication, and the puck’s surface works like a trackpad to move the onscreen cursor. That seems much smoother than reaching out to control the device with hand movements, but the trackpad wasn't very precise either. Which is a shame, as it would be ideal for someone on an airplane, say, who wants to control the device without punching the seat in front of them.

Controls are the biggest problem I’ve had with the Aura. The front cameras track your hand movements. Hold out your hand and pinch two fingers together to open up an app or move a window. It works most of the time, but some gestures don’t always register. I find myself trying to open Spotify or switch between titles on Prime Video and have to repeatedly pinch the air in front of me for anything to happen. When people have been around to see me, they’ve told me I look like I’ve gone bonkers, just grunting and wildly pinching thin air.

According to recent reports, the Xreal Aura glasses are a stunning display of how far smart-glasses technology has come. But they still feel like a novelty that most people won’t want or need. They haven’t quite solved the core issues facing the product category—looking like a dork or being effortlessly comfortable to wear. But they do feel like a major step in the right direction. If only they could get a pinch more usable.

Taking Korea's toughest exam from behind bars

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1706 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The boys in Mandela have been convicted of serious offences.
  • Students intently focus on maths formulas written on a board before lowering their heads and taking notes as the teacher works through a sum.
  • The teacher's voice and the scratch of pens fill the room.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The boys in Mandela have been convicted of serious offences.

Students intently focus on maths formulas written on a board before lowering their heads and taking notes as the teacher works through a sum.

The teacher's voice and the scratch of pens fill the room.

At first glance, this could be any classroom in South Korea.

But thick metal bars cover the windows and the students are wearing blue prison uniforms and rubber shoes emblazoned with the words "Korea Correctional Service".

This is Mandela Boys' School, an education facility for young prisoners inside the Seoul Southern Correctional Institution in Guro, south-west Seoul. In South Korea, young people who are sentenced to imprisonment by a criminal court must serve their time in prison.

"The boys here have committed serious offences and received criminal sentences," Jeong Yeo-gyeong, a correctional officer in the Korea Correctional Service's social reintegration division, told the BBC.

"As well as theft, there is a high proportion of serious offences, including violence, bodily injury, sexual violence and robbery.".

But by opening educational institutes like Mandela, authorities are hoping to give these young offenders a chance to better their lives after they serve out their sentences.

Opened by the justice ministry in March 2023, it allows boys who were aged 17 and under when their sentences became final to prepare for school equivalency exams as well as the Suneung - the country's notoriously difficult university entrance examination - while still serving their sentences.

Held every November, the Suneung is an infamous eight-hour marathon of back-to-back exams.

Students attempt about 200 questions across various subjects, which include Korean, maths, English, social and natural sciences, among others.

The country itself comes to a standstill - construction work halts, planes are grounded and military training gets suspended to facilitate an optimal testing environment.

A total of 551,864 people have applied to take this year's Suneung on 19 November.

Around 30 prisoners are enrolled in the Suneung preparation class at Mandela Boys' School, and 11 of them have applied to take this year's exam.

Several boys are sitting the Suneung exam this year and are taking intensive preparation classes.

Park Soo-young (not his real name), a 17-year-old inmate, has been at the Mandela Boys' Suneung preparation class for two months and hopes to study social welfare.

He tells the BBC that he had dreams of becoming a police officer before committing the crime that landed him behind bars.

Sources indicate that he states he could not bring himself to look properly at his mother during his trial. When he turned towards her after his sentence was announced, she was crying.

Sources indicate that "Seeing her like that, I broke down too. I wondered how I was going to live from then on, and how I could look after my mother, who was on her own. I think I kept crying for about a week while I was in the detention centre.".

Industry observers note that looking back on his offence, he says he feels "very ashamed that I couldn't control that impulse". If he could meet his younger self, he would tell him: "Control that impulse. If you do, everything will be different.".

"I'd grab myself by the collar and shake myself as I stated it.".

He hopes the Suneung and university will offer him a chance to start again.

It has been revealed that "Once I'm out, I need to cut ties with the friends and people I used to know and start a upcoming life. I think university is the only way to do that. Going to university would let me leave the area where I used to live, move somewhere else and start something new. That's why I began studying again.".

But he describes beginning Suneung preparation as "a struggle every day".

According to recent reports, "But the teachers don't let anything slip past. They keep helping us until we understand. If I don't understand something, I put my hand up and they come over and explain it.

According to recent reports, sometimes, if I've missed something, I keep working at it on my own. If I still can't get it, I ask the students next to me to explain," he stated.

Park's day begins at 06:30 with a morning check by prison officers. He starts memorising English vocabulary and working through Korean reading passages early in the morning.

It has been revealed that "I learn English words whenever I can, even before breakfast. From 07:00, I work through a Korean passage, something like literature or speech. We have to come down to the classroom at 08:00, so we have another check and then come down for lessons.".

Recent findings suggest that during breaks, students make calls to their families or leave the classroom for scheduled visits. In the evening, they return for supervised study. Once the day's activities are over, they must go back to their cells together.

Park says he studies until 22:00 before finishing for the day. If he wants to study longer hours, he needs permission from a prison officer.

According to recent reports, but even if gets a good result this year, Park will not be allowed to leave prison and attend university straight away. He is only due to be released in 2028, but plans to use this exam as experience and continue studying next year.

Recent findings suggest that "This time, I want to experience how the Suneung works and how competitive it is. Then, next year, I'll work hard from the start so I can get in the year after that.".

By opening educational institutes like Mandela, authorities are hoping to give young offenders a chance to better their lives.

Some former students from Mandela Boys' School have managed to get into university, according to the justice ministry.

Others have continued their studies after leaving prison, including by enrolling in residential exam preparation academies.

The inmates are taught by a team of seven prison officers, all of whom hold teaching certificates. Each is responsible for a subject.

Industry observers note that visiting instructors provide classes in the humanities, arts and sport, while university student volunteers help with learning. Professional psychological counselling is also available.

Recent findings suggest that park Min-yong, who applied to work here in 2023, teaches science. And alongside Suneung lessons, he works with the students' to change their habits and behaviour.

One thing he often tells them is that they need to "learn how to become adults".

He believes that while studying in itself does not necessarily turn inmates away from a life of crime, the experience of having worked hard at something: staying with a concept that makes little sense, revisiting a wrong answer and continuing even when grades do not improve straight away, is valuable in itself.

"Studying properly means pushing yourself to your limits, and that takes considerable stamina and patience," he indicates.

"Whether they chose to do it or not, the experience of persevering, enduring and not giving up easily may help them to some extent when they face the difficulties of life after release.".

He indicates the material they encounter while preparing for the Suneung also gives them newly introduced things to think about.

It has been revealed that korean reading passages cover literature, society, science and philosophy. Students have to consider a character's perspective, examine the evidence behind an argument and understand unfamiliar concepts. They also encounter explanations that differ from their own and have to reconsider what they think.

"They gradually learn that it's not just about their own personal view - that these concepts and relationships have been developed through a shared understanding among many people," Park said.

There are difficult moments too.

Park indicates students sometimes cheat in classroom tests even while he is watching.

"They cheat as if it's nothing. They give each other answers, even when I'm watching them. Some repeat it after being told off. There may be an element of doing it deliberately, but often they haven't thought it through. They don't think about the impact their actions or words could have on others.".

The boys also have a strong desire for recognition, he indicates.

Recent findings suggest that "It's all the time. 'Look how much I've done. Look how much my grades have improved. I've done this much - haven't I done well?' They're always like that. They're hungry for it.".

Park Min-yong teaches science to the boys in Mandela.

Not everyone agrees with this initiative though.

One criticism is that young people who have not committed crimes also face fierce competition for university places: so there is some anger that the state provides offenders with separate education and opportunities to prepare for this exam.

Father Jeong Min-ha, of the Archdiocese of Seoul's correctional ministry committee, worked with Seoul Southern Correctional Institution from September 2023 until last year.

He acknowledges these criticisms.

"Studying gives them a sense of achievement and time to look seriously at their own lives. That's why I think it matters. I think that is the most important part of rehabilitation.".

Of course, there is no guarantee.

Park recalls a student who had done well at the school but later returned to prison.

"He was doing well when he left, but in the end he came back. So something went wrong. I'd hoped he would carry on with what he'd been doing here, but he couldn't. That's disappointing.".

According to recent reports, according to the justice ministry's 2026 corrections statistical yearbook, 35.5% of prisoners aged under 20 who were released in 2021 were imprisoned again within three years. That was about 1.7 times the overall rate of 21.2%, and the highest of any age group.

But Park hopes the students will continue learning after they leave prison. "We don't know what the outcome will be," he indicates.

Sources indicate that "They say the way to clear a glass of dirty water is to keep pouring clean water into it, rather than trying to remove each bit of dirt. I hope they fill their minds with good things, learn to use their energy and intellect in the right way, and put that learning into practice at the right time and place.".

Additional reporting by Hosu Lee.

Industry News: Apple adds new disk controls to prevent AI agents from running amok
