⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Mac users will be warned of the risks of granting AI full disk access.
  • According to recent reports, after sounding an alarm about the concern last month, Apple is taking steps to limit Mac disk access to AI agents, the firm declared on its developer blog.
  • The issue rose to prominence in September, when Inc.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Mac users will be warned of the risks of granting AI full disk access.

According to recent reports, after sounding an alarm about the concern last month, Apple is taking steps to limit Mac disk access to AI agents, the firm declared on its developer blog. In its latest macOS beta, Apple introduced controls to ensure that consumers will need to take "very explicit" actions to grant apps like ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini "this extraordinary level of [full disk] access.".

The issue rose to prominence in September, when Inc. columnist Jason Aten noticed that Meta's Muse Mac app was able to access his messages even though he thought he had denied that permission. Meta argued that Aten must have granted access, saying the feature is entirely opt-in, but the incident caught Apple's eye. "Some developers are using Full Disk Access in ways that could put users at risk, exposing everything on their systems — including files, mail, messages, and even browsing history — without users' full knowledge and understanding," Apple wrote.

Recent findings suggest that apple vowed to address the issue with fresh disk controls. As screen grabs from X user @madeby_ldt show, Apple's Full Disk Access setting now requires explicit permissions to be granted from a scary-looking pop-up screen. It states, "Your Mac will not be able to protect your data from [your desired AI app]," and forces you to review and OK the actions it will be able to take. Those include "Read, Change, Delete and Export all your Data," "View Hidden and Recently Deleted Photos," and "View History and Browser as You.".

The new controls won't stop people from granting AI agents access to your files, but it should give them pause. If one of those AI agents goes rogue — which is something we've seen before — they could potentially leak or misuse your private data. Stopping this is key for Mac models like the Studio that Apple is specifically marketing for local AI models and agents.

"As AI agents become increasingly capable and autonomous, the risks associated with this level of access will grow substantially. We are committed to ensuring users clearly understand these risks before granting such access, so they can make informed decisions about their own data and privacy," Apple stated last month. The upcoming feature is now out on macOS 27.3 beta 2, but there's no word on when it will be released to all users.

Breaking: Jensen Huang allies build a "war room" to get him back at Nvidia

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Jensen Huang is considering a comeback as Nvidia’s chief executive, as allies in Silicon Valley pressure the manufacturer’s board to reinstate him days after the tech executive resigned over reports he had affairs with a suspected Chinese spy and a subordinate.
  • Huang has discussed with confidants the possibility of returning, according to multiple people familiar with the matter—even as an independent probe by Nvidia’s board investigates the conduct that led to a spectacular leadership crisis at the $4 trillion chip organization this week.
  • One Huang ally told the FT they were putting together a “war room” of Silicon Valley executives to lobby for the former Nvidia chief’s return and would try to garner support from the White House.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Jensen Huang is considering a comeback as Nvidia’s chief executive, as allies in Silicon Valley pressure the manufacturer’s board to reinstate him days after the tech executive resigned over reports he had affairs with a suspected Chinese spy and a subordinate.

Huang has discussed with confidants the possibility of returning, according to multiple people familiar with the matter—even as an independent probe by Nvidia’s board investigates the conduct that led to a spectacular leadership crisis at the $4 trillion chip organization this week.

One Huang ally told the FT they were putting together a “war room” of Silicon Valley executives to lobby for the former Nvidia chief’s return and would try to garner support from the White House.

“Everyone that matters in tech outside the frontier labs loves Jensen,” they stated. The efforts had Huang’s support, they added.

A public campaign to reinstate Huang has gathered steam over the weekend. Tesla and SpaceX chief Elon Musk and Epic Games chief executive Tim Sweeney were among executives backing a public letter demanding that its board “Bring Jensen Back.”.

Huang continues to command fierce loyalty from some employees, several of whom have gone public in calling for his return in the days since he resigned and have signed the open letter.

The effort to reinstate Huang is likely to face pushback from key policymakers in Washington, with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Sunday calling for a “dramatic shake-up” in leadership at the company after Huang’s departure.

Huang, who lacked the controlling shareholding of other founder-CEOs and was therefore unable to overule any board decision, also faces a board and a management team now led by interim chief executive Colette Kress that is aiming to steady the firm ahead of quarterly results on Tuesday.

Huang’s affair with Alice Huang, an executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed, has triggered deepening scrutiny of Nvidia’s compliance measures when selling its AI chips to customers in Asia who have potential links to China.

Even allies were unsure how to rehabilitate Huang’s reputation. “Having an affair with a subordinate is a fireable offense,” acknowledged one person involved in efforts to reinstate Huang.

Sources indicate that the FT reported on Friday that Arm chief Rene Haas has been approached by Nvidia’s board as a potential successor. Nvidia’s board said no “formal” process had been initiated.

Altimeter Capital founder Brad Gerstner and Atreides Management boss Gavin Baker—who are Nvidia shareholders—published an open letter to the board on Friday urging them to leave “all options on the table, including the potential return of Jensen Huang.”.

The pair, both large investors in the manufacturer, cited “the extraordinary success of Jensen Huang’s leadership over a long period of time and given the massive uncertainty associated with recent events surrounding his departure” as reasons for clemency.

Voldemort, Gotham City and the Greens: Victorian election gets a jolt of life as leaders face off in sole debate

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1141 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theguardian

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Ben Carroll, Jess Wilson, Ellen Sandell and Warren Pickering grilled by undecided voters – and each other – as state prepares to head to the polls.
  • For a brief moment on Tuesday night, the Victorian election looked like it might actually get interesting.
  • Two weeks into the offical campaign, with early voting opening on Wednesday, the contest has been pretty short on excitement.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ben Carroll, Jess Wilson, Ellen Sandell and Warren Pickering grilled by undecided voters – and each other – as state prepares to head to the polls.

For a brief moment on Tuesday night, the Victorian election looked like it might actually get interesting.

Two weeks into the offical campaign, with early voting opening on Wednesday, the contest has been pretty short on excitement. The Labor government has continued to slide in the polls, while the Coalition opposition has largely been focused on not getting in its own way for long enough to cruise to victory.

But the only debate of the campaign offered a welcome jolt of life. Dubbed the “People’s Forum” by hosts News24 and the Herald Sun, Tuesday evening’s showdown delivered a few moments of political theatre.

There was the moment the opposition leader, Jess Wilson, mocked the premier, Ben Carroll, for refusing to say the names of his predecessors, Daniel Andrews and Jacinta Allan, telling the Labor leader they’re “not Voldemort”.

“I can say their name just as you can say Jeff Kennett’s name,” Carroll responded.

“Jeff Kennett,” Wilson immediately retorted.

(For all the back-and-forth, Carroll never did say their names).

Industry observers note that or Wilson’s apparent “Julia Gillard moment”, according to the Herald Sun, when she told Carroll she “would not be lectured” by him on the costings of her policies. The premier had claimed the Liberal intends didn’t “stack up” and would require cuts to healthcare funding to pay down debt.

“I like to see these scare campaigns that you run,” Wilson noted. “But Ben, I won’t be lectured by you or your government on costings when you have racked up $200bn worth of debt in this state.”.

Then there was One Nation’s Victorian leader, Warren Pickering, who noted the state resembled “Gotham City” because of rising crime and vowed to lock up more offenders – even if that meant sending them interstate.

Industry observers note that “I don’t give a damn if our prisons are full. You’ve broken the law. You’re going to jail. They’re bringing in a supermax in Latest South Wales. That’s where you’re bloody going,” he mentioned.

The only person to receive rousing applause was Billy, a bearded schoolteacher who asked how the leaders planned to rebuild trust in politics when, as he put it: “Nobody believes a word you say any more – and it’s fundamental. No fun, and mostly mental.”.

But many of the night’s most memorable moments came courtesy of Greens leader, Ellen Sandell, whose late inclusion on the panel followed a stoush between Carroll and Wilson over whether Pickering should be invited.

“Having four of us on the stage tonight tells you everything about how politics is changing,” Sandell told the 100 undecided voters gathered at the Sofitel in Melbourne.

In her green blazer, and unmistakably in enemy territory, Sandell spoke authentically and was the only leader willing to take all three other parties to task: Labor over donations from the gambling industry, the Liberals over money from property developers and One Nation for its links to billionaire Gina Rinehart, who she said is “writing [their] policy”.

“If you’re wondering why you can’t afford your groceries or your rent or to buy a home, just look at who is funding these three other parties,” Sandell said.

When offered the opportunity to ask any other leader a question, Sandell asked Carroll how he can claim to fight for working people given cuts to the public sector and fights with health workers, teachers, council workers and firefighters over wages.

She also engaged in a back and forth with Wilson on several challenges. Asked whether she would possibly support the Liberals with confidence and supply in the event of a hung parliament, she stated the Greens values were “quite far apart” from the Coalition’s: “Jess Wilson wants to rip up treaty. She wants to rip up renewable energy. She wants to make sigfniciant cuts to public service.”.

Wilson relied on an often repeated line that treaty “goes far further than what the voice [to parliament] ever did” and “undermines our parliament”.

Sandell’s response: “You know that’s not true though, you can’t lie to the Victorian people like that.”.

The pair also clashed over pro-Palestinian protests in Melbourne’s CBD, with Sandell defending the right to “peaceful protest”.

“There is a very clear difference between antisemitism, which is unacceptable, and actually standing up and calling out war crimes that are happening by the government of Israel,” she noted.

Wilson responded: “At these protests, we have seen people throw rocks at police officers. That is not a peaceful protest.

Sandell responded that existing laws already dealt with such incidents and argued that protest permits were not the answer.

“Politicians shouldn’t be the ones deciding who gets to protest,” she noted. “That is an authoritarian government move, and we do not want that.”.

Pickering agreed with Sandell and stated politicians should not be deciding who gets to protest. He described One Nation as a “flagbearer” for the principles of democracy, including freedom of speech.

“I don’t necessarily think the permits are the way to go,” he said.

Wilson, who holds a comfortable lead in the polls, arguably had the most to lose from the debate but held her own. She largely avoided taking the bait from the other leaders, including Pickering, who during his turn to ask a question, tried to pressure her on the Coalition’s position on legislated net zero targets. Wilson stuck to her line that she was governed by “practicality” and “not ideology”.

She was less definitive on the Suburban Rail Loop, leaving open the possibility of scrapping the multibillion-dollar project once the Coalition had “visibility” of the contracts that have been signed.

Asked by moderator Kieran Gilbert if the Coalition would be willing to scrap the project and move on, Wilson said: “That’s exactly what the review is for.”.

Carroll, meanwhile, acknowledged that Labor had made mistakes during its 12 years in government but leaned heavily on its record, including 121 fresh schools, record NAPLAN results, the highest-paid teachers in the country and 17,000 nurses.

He also repeatedly referred to his decision to call a royal commission into allegations of corruption on government construction sites, describing it as one of the “hardest” things he had done.

Victoria will not get another leaders debate, after Carroll and Wilson failed to agree on terms for one on free-to-air television.

In a recent development, the audience members were polled as they left the Sofitel, with 39% saying Wilson had won the debate, followed by Sandell on 25% and Pickering on 16%. Just 13% were undecided at the end of the night and only 7% picked Carroll.

It appears no matter what the premier has to say, many Victorians have stopped listening.

Benita Kolovos is Guardian Australia’s Victorian state correspondent.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Austrian authorities have taken initial steps to revoke the citizenship of a former foreign minister who moved to Russia — a country she has lauded for its “genuine freedom” — and who has repeatedly denigrated Austria while echoing Kremlin-friendly talking points.

Karin Kneissl made international headlines when she danced with President Vladimir Putin of Russia at her wedding in 2018, when she was her nation’s top diplomat.

Since then, she has angered many of her compatriots with regular barbs against her country of birth and its citizens.

That the Austrian state would even consider the extraordinary step of revoking her citizenship reflects a national weariness about the former foreign minister. It follows a prolonged national debate over whether Ms. Kneissl retained the right to remain Austrian after — both physically and by all appearances ideologically — turning her back on her homeland.

Industry observers note that ms. Kneissl, who served as foreign minister from 2017 to 2019, made her very public move to Russia in 2023, a year after Russia debuted its full-scale invasion of Ukraine. She was hired to run a think tank in St. Petersburg.

Industry observers note that over the years, Ms. Kneissl, 61, seems to have taken pleasure in denigrating Austrians in interviews with Russian-friendly media. Earlier this year, for example, she repeated her claim that Hitler, who was born in Austria, was typically Austrian. She also noted that her countrymen had acted like hyenas toward her.

Recent findings suggest that such comments served to bolster a push to strip her of her citizenship. The initiative has been led by the liberal party NEOS, which is run by the current foreign minister, Beate Meinl-Reisinger.

“Why does Kneissl continue to appear prominently as Austria’s former foreign minister when she so obviously despises and hates our country?” Yannick Shetty, a NEOS member of the Austrian Parliament, asked in January in response to Ms. Kneissl’s remarks.

On Monday, officials in Vienna confirmed that an inquiry into the former minister had been launched. They said they were looking at whether she had obtained a second citizenship and whether her conduct significantly harmed “the interests or reputation of the Republic.”.

It remains unclear if the inquiry will actually lead to the revocation of her citizenship and, if so, how long it might take.

Ms. Kneissl was proposed for the post of foreign minister in 2017 by the far-right Freedom Party of Austria, though she was never a member of that party.

After leaving Austria in 2020, she went to France and Lebanon before moving to a little village southeast of Moscow in the heartland of Russia.

On Monday, Ms. Kneissl mentioned she knew that steps were being taken to revoke her citizenship. In comments reported by the Russian state news agency Tass, she said that if Austria moved forward with the blueprint, she would end up stateless and need to apply for travel documents from the United Nations.

Christopher F. Schuetze is a reporter for The Times based in Berlin, covering politics, society and culture in Germany, Austria and Switzerland.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It’s mounted in a handmade wooden frame and will be released in limited numbers.

According to recent reports, TRMNL, the manufacturer known for e-paper frames and kits, just released its biggest and most colorful product yet. Frame is a 31.5-inch full color e-paper display mounted in a handmade wooden frame, designed to show paintings, photos, maps, graphics and other still images in a more natural way than LCD or OLED screens. Though not cheap, it features high-quality materials and will be released in limited numbers to start with.

If you've never heard of TRMNL, the tech giant has had some buzz of late with its e-paper displays sold in frames or kits. Thus far, products like the DIY (kit) and OG (picture frame) have been strictly black and white or grayscale, because "TRMNL is not a television. We avoid trying to do too much," founder Ryan Kulp explained in a blog post.

However, the introduction of grayscale with the OG model apparently got the manufacturer thinking that color "aligns with our vision and just maybe, it makes it even better," Kulp wrote. To that end, TRMNL introduced the full-color e-paper Frame, set to ship by late 2026 or early 2027 for $1,300 in a first batch of around 470 units.

Sources indicate that "Over the past few months we've been developing Lazarus, a color conversion engine that we think provides Frame the best color matching on the market for any Spectra 6 display," Kulp wrote. "And yes it will be open source for your own tuning pleasure.".

To further improve picture quality, Frame will use clock sync to reduce flicker and extend battery life. Though internet connected, it offers a microSD port if you prefer to run it offline. Along with a rechargeable battery, you get a rear USB-C port with a small hole through the back panel for always-on connectivity. It can be hung in portrait or landscape orientation, and you can optionally buy or build your own kickstand.

Industry observers note that TRMNL is working on community developers on other features and even "created a Local Art plugin where anyone can submit their work and even sell it through the TRMNL platform." The organization promises a transparent supply chain and has everything it needs to build Frame "in stock or on order" for a smooth fulfillment cycle. Everything is assembled by its team and not outsourced.

Pre-orders are now open starting at $1,300, with the first batch shipping to the USA, Canada, Mexico and Australia. Potential buyers outside those countries can still get in on the action by pre-ordering here, though the TRMNL noted that "duty/import fees could be quite high given the product's customs value." Next year, it plans to open another woodworking shop near its Berlin warehouse to offer "postage- and duty-free fulfillment.".

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Hadiza left school at 13 to get married and now spends her time doing housework.

Recent findings suggest that as she pounds millet, 15-year-old Hadiza sings the English alphabet. It is a reminder of something that she desperately misses - going to school.

"Sometimes I write on the ground to practise and see if I'm still writing correctly," she indicates.

One night, about two years ago, a group of armed men raided her village.

Recent findings suggest that "They scared our cattle away and abducted a girl. We had to run away. We walked barefoot all the way here," she claims.

Since then she has lived in a displaced persons camp in Goronyo, a few kilometres from her home. For a short while she went to school here, but soon met a young man and, at the age of 13, stopped going to classes and got married.

"It's tradition here that once a girl is married, her education ends," she explains.

Now she lives with her in-laws and helps look after the home.

Although Nigerian law prohibits marriage under the age of 18, it is not always enforced.

Hadiza practises writing on the ground to make sure she doesn't forget the English alphabet.

According to recent reports, hadiza is one of nearly 19 million children in Nigeria who are missing out on an education, according to estimates shared by Unesco in 2024. That's about one in four of the country's school-age children.

Against this backdrop, the BBC World Service has launched Dars Hausa, an educational programme in the main language spoken in northern Nigeria, as well as neighbouring Niger, Cameroon and elsewhere in West Africa.

According to recent reports, it brings English, maths and science lessons to children across West Africa, via social media, local television partnerships and radio. Many people in the region get their news from the radio and nearly half of households in Nigeria have one, according to the charity Save the Children.

According to recent reports, dars means "lesson" in Pashto and Dari, and it was first launched in those languages in 2023 for Afghan children barred from attending school. An Arabic version followed in February 2025.

The reasons why so many Nigerian children are out of school are numerous and complex. Like Hadiza, 12-year-old Rukayya also lives in the displacement camp in Goronyo.

After Rukayya's father was killed, she gave up school to earn money instead.

"It pains me to see other children studying and going to school while I cannot," she says.

As the eldest child, each day Rukayya goes out to gather firewood to sell and to beg so that her younger siblings can have something to eat.

"If my father was alive, I wouldn't have to go out and beg," she explains, saying some people mock her "but it doesn't stop me because it is our only way to survive.".

Bandits killed her father about a year ago in front of her, she says, and her family fled from their home to the camp.

She and Hadiza are among 670,000 people in north-west and central Nigeria who have been forced from their homes by armed robbery and kidnappings, according to the International Organization for Migration.

Three Girls: Lessons in Limbo features the stories of Hadiza and Rukayya - you can watch the full film on YouTube, external.

Some attacks have been carried out by militant Islamist groups, but the majority in this region are by criminal gangs, known in Nigeria as bandits, who steal, kill and kidnap.

The school that Hadiza once attended in Goronyo is the only one serving children in the camp and typically has about 50 students in each class.

One of the teachers, Kamilu Sulaiman Jakada, says that even though lessons are free, only a tiny portion of the children attend, and even then sporadically, because parents tell him that "it is the children that are the breadwinners" and they need to earn money to eat.

Armed gangs, poverty and lack of funding all have a huge impact on children's education, states teacher Kamilu Sulaiman Jakada.

He says the school does not have enough teachers or classrooms, explaining that funding is inconsistent and often comes from individuals or organisations rather than the government.

The other challenge is the bandits. A gang once came to the school on motorbikes, shooting in the air, he indicates, and although no-one was hurt, many parents were scared and withdrew their children. That has been parents' reaction to attacks in some other parts of the country too.

Sources indicate that every Nigerian child is meant to get nine years of free, compulsory education - six in primary and three in secondary school. Responsibility is shared between federal, state and local governments.

But many schools are facing shortages and poorer families who cannot afford private education can struggle to pay for uniforms, books and transport.

The crisis has built up over decades, with successive governments struggling to address chronic underfunding and poor oversight of resources.

In addition, many children in the traditional Almajiri system, which provides Islamic education, are not taught subjects such as maths and science, and are considered by Unicef to be out of school.

Many of Nigeria's schools face shortages of teachers, classrooms and learning materials after years of underfunding and lack of oversight.

Minister of State for Education Prof Suwaiba Sa'id believes the number of children out of school is lower than has been reported, but admits that with Nigeria's growing population "the proper investment, the proper oversight, has not been doneâ¦ I will not mention the names, but we know of two states that did not recruit a single teacher for eight years".

She says that education is the government's "number-one priority" and initiatives such as Lumina are designed to help address "decades of neglect". Lumina aims to support one million girls by 2030, providing an accelerated learning programme for older girls who have missed years of formal education.

She also indicates that "the government is doing everything possible" to deal with bandits and that "we have seen children that should be at school but are engaged in this banditry".

According to recent reports, in the meantime, it is children like Hadiza and Rukayya that the BBC World Service Dars Hausa programmes aim to help. Hadiza says she still has a dream to one day become a doctor "to help my fellow women".

Industry observers note that dars Hausa will air on BBC News Hausa radio on Sundays at 06:45 West Africa Time, with a repeat at 20:45. The programme will also be available via BBC News Hausa's digital platforms, including YouTube, Facebook, X and Instagram.

Breaking: Australia’s gender pay gap falls below 20% for first time

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Men still dominate top-paid positions but businesses’ ‘deliberate’ decisions have narrowed gap, workplace gender equality agency report finds.
  • Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast.
  • Australian women earn 80c for every $1 men earn, on average, after Australia’s gender pay gap fell below 20% for the first time in 2025-26.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Men still dominate top-paid positions but businesses’ ‘deliberate’ decisions have narrowed gap, workplace gender equality agency report finds.

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast.

Australian women earn 80c for every $1 men earn, on average, after Australia’s gender pay gap fell below 20% for the first time in 2025-26.

The workplace gender equality agency’s (WGEA) report on Wednesday showed men still dominated top-paid positions but businesses’ decisions have narrowed the gap.

WGEA chief Christine Castley said most Australian employers were ignoring backlash to diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) and improving their hiring and promotion to ensure women reached senior positions.

“Employers are actually thinking in a very deliberate way about what’s going on with workplace gender equality and then taking action,” Castley told Guardian Australia.

The overall WGEA pay gap was 19.7% for the year, with the 2025-26 survey including federal government public sector employers for the first time.

It has been revealed that the figure has improved significantly in the last decade, from 26.3% in 2015-16. Coverage has also increased, now covering more than 6m employees across 9,096 employers.

The private sector’s pay gap fell from 21.1% last year to 20.3% this year, as women accounted for a growing share of full-time management and leadership roles.

Bigger pay rises in female-dominated industries, including retail, aged care and childcare, also helped narrow the gap.

However, women-dominated industries and occupations were still typically paid less than those dominated by men. The average woman still earned $27,467 less per year than the average man, WGEA found.

In a recent development, the survey accounted not only for wages but all earnings, including penalty rates, superannuation, bonuses and overtime. Average total remuneration in the survey was $125,568.

The overall distribution of pay did not improve from 2024-25. Women make up about half of Australia’s workforce but men remained overrepresented in the highest-paid positions.

In a recent development, every level of management was dominated by men, WGEA found. The disparity was greatest at the chief executive level, where three in four CEOs were men and the gender pay gap widened to 27.6%.

It has been revealed that women accounted for just 36% of employees in the top pay quartile in the private sector. In the commonwealth public sector, women’s representation in the top quartile was 46% and the gender pay gap was just 7.8%.

Promotion rates are similar between genders but women are less represented at higher levels, likely because they resign or take time off for care and domestic responsibilities, previous WGEA work has found.

It has been revealed that wednesday’s report found just 7% of manager roles are part-time, but 29% of women work part-time compared with 12% of men. WGEA called for workplaces to redesign roles to allow more part-time work.

In the financial services sector, which has the worst pay gap at 26.7%, men would be more likely to be promoted or get bonuses as they took on more visible work, Castley noted.

“[It’s] the person who can attend the client functions [and] can be available 24/7, the person who’s most visible to the leadership of the organisation, versus, perhaps, the person [doing] the work that’s behind the scenes,” Castley remarked.

Superannuation provider Rest was an outlier in the finance industry. Its pay gap has fallen to 9.4%, from 20.1% in 2022.

Rest’s chief people officer, Amy Murrell, said the improvements had been helped by extending paid parental leave to all permanent staff, regardless of gender, time of arrival or primary or secondary carer classification.

“It’s not going to happen naturally,” Murrell remarked. “I think you have to prioritise it for it to make sense.”.

The firm had also increased representation after setting targets for at least 40% of employees to be women and 40% men at every level of its business, from its board to its investment team.

Castley stated some Australian business leaders had taken on an “anti-DEI” narrative, amid global backlash to diversity, equity and inclusion measures, but most businesses were “getting on with the job”.

WGEA asked businesses to set fresh targets for the first time in 2026. The most popular goals included improving gender balance at junior and managerial levels and consulting employees on gender equality efforts.

“These are the real problems that need to be tackled … and it’s actually very reassuring that those are the targets that employers have picked because it demonstrates, I think, a very real commitment to actually taking action,” Castley said.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Health officials in Pennsylvania and Wisconsin revealed two more measles deaths late last week, bringing the national tally of confirmed measles deaths this year to 10. The total includes the deaths of at least four infants: two in Pennsylvania, one in Newly introduced York, and one in Wisconsin.

Wisconsin health officials remarked the latest measles death—the second for the state—was in a child. Pennsylvania’s health department did not reveal the age or other details of the latest death—the state’s seventh—besides revealing it was of an unvaccinated resident in Montour County. Overall, the seven deaths in Pennsylvania include two in Jefferson County, three in Lancaster County, and one in Mifflin, in addition to the fresh death in Montour. An eighth death was reported in Franklin County, but state health officials have not confirmed it.

For all the states with deaths so far, health officials have noted that they’re the first deaths in decades. Multiple outbreaks are underway across the country, pushing the national tally of cases to nearly 5,500 across 47 states and jurisdictions, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Pennsylvania’s case count alone is over 1,500, and Wisconsin is reporting nearly 650.

It has been revealed that with outbreaks that have been smoldering and flaring since last year, the US has reportedly lost its measles elimination status—as medical and public health experts have widely expected it would. A panel of experts for the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO), a regional branch of the World Health Organization, convened last week to review US measles data and assess its elimination status. The PAHO is set to announce its conclusion and the review’s other findings on Tuesday, November 17. But sources broke the news to The Wall Street Journal on Friday that the panel had found that the US had indeed lost its status.

It has been revealed that an elimination status is determined by international health authorities after a country has gone more than 12 months without continuous spread of a virus. The status is lost when epidemiological and laboratory data indicate that a chain of transmission involving a viral strain with an identical genotype and lineage has continued uninterrupted for 12 months or longer.

It has been revealed that the US earned its elimination status in 2000 after hard-fought vaccination campaigns over several decades. But US vaccination rates have slipped below protective levels in recent years, fueled by the rise of anti-vaccine rhetoric and vaccine misinformation from fierce anti-vaccine advocates, including current US Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. As vaccination rates slipped, measles cases skyrocketed. The current case tally is the highest seen since 1991.

Industry observers note that in reporting the PAHO’s determination, the Journal quoted Noel Brewer, chair of an independent US committee who presented findings about the country’s measles outbreaks to PAHO, on the country’s lamentable status: “Runaway measles outbreaks in the United States, as well as the needless deaths, are all due to low measles vaccination coverage. We’ve gotten comfortable letting children be stopped by a deadly disease and die from it.”.

The US Department of Health and Human Services did not immediately respond to requests to comment about the loss of the elimination status or to answer a question about how anti-vaccine rhetoric and misinformation, including that from Kennedy, has contributed.

Industry observers note that medical and public health experts continue to sharply criticize Kennedy’s and the Trump administration’s poor handling of the ongoing severe outbreaks. The CDC has not held press briefings in efforts to halt the vaccine-preventable illness and promote vaccination. Instead, Kennedy reportedly ordered the CDC to remove measles death data, and the CDC director declined to approve an urgent health alert about the life-threatening risks of measles during pregnancy.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Almost two weeks after the Democrats swept to victory in the midterm elections, votes are still being counted in the race to elect a senator in Alaska, with Democratic candidate Mary Peltola ahead of her Republican rival - Senator Dan S Sullivan.
  • This Senate contest has drawn scrutiny after another Dan Sullivan entered the race earlier this year - with ballot papers listing both the incumbent Dan S Sullivan and a Daniel J Sullivan Jr.
  • Republicans have said this could have confused voters, prompting an unsuccessful legal challenge and President Donald Trump claiming votes for "the fake Dan Sullivan" were supposed to be for "the real Dan Sullivan".
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Almost two weeks after the Democrats swept to victory in the midterm elections, votes are still being counted in the race to elect a senator in Alaska, with Democratic candidate Mary Peltola ahead of her Republican rival - Senator Dan S Sullivan.

This Senate contest has drawn scrutiny after another Dan Sullivan entered the race earlier this year - with ballot papers listing both the incumbent Dan S Sullivan and a Daniel J Sullivan Jr.

Republicans have said this could have confused voters, prompting an unsuccessful legal challenge and President Donald Trump claiming votes for "the fake Dan Sullivan" were supposed to be for "the real Dan Sullivan".

US media has not forecasted a winner in the race - the last Senate seat still without a winner after the 3 November election.

But with 98% of the vote counted, even if Senator Dan S Sullivan's votes were combined with Daniel J Sullivan Jr's votes, this would still not overcome Peltola's lead.

Alaska uses a ranked-choice voting system, which means voters can vote for five candidates in order of preference. If no candidate reaches more than 50% of the first preference votes, then voters' other choices will be used to decide who wins.

Industry observers note that BBC Verify has analysed voting data showing voters' second choices. It indicates that over a third of voters who put Daniel J Sullivan Jr first left their second choice blank.

The next highest second-choice preference was for the Democratic candidate Mary Peltola - receiving nearly twice as many second-choice votes as the Republican Dan S Sullivan.

This calls into question claims that Republican voters may have been confused about which Sullivan they were voting for.

Why midterm vote-counting is taking so long in America's largest state.

Republican Dan S Sullivan has held the US Senate seat in Alaska since 2015 and was running for his third term.

Daniel J Sullivan Jr - a retired school teacher from a remote fishing village in Alaska - entered the race in May and has run a low-key campaign.

A Fresh York Times story, external published the week before Election Day claimed that Democratic operatives with links to the Peltola campaign had tried to recruit "spoiler" candidates in the Senate race, including Daniel J Sullivan Jr.

Sources indicate that the report stated it had seen text messages and interviewed 12 people who participated in or were told of the plan, or were would-be candidates who the team also tried to recruit. The BBC has not independently verified the reporting.

Peltola has denied all knowledge of the alleged "scheme" and Sullivan Jr has denied any links with the Peltola campaign.

President Trump has posted multiple times on Truth Social since the election, claiming that the race has been "rigged".

But experts note it's not an illegal tactic, if it was employed.

"There is nothing to prevent a campaign from recruiting someone else to run, even if for political reasons," said Joshua Douglas, an election law expert at the University of Kentucky.

Alaska Senate candidate denies knowing about alleged plot to put two Dan Sullivans on ballot.

Senator Sullivan was joined by President Trump at a campaign rally ahead of the vote.

Voters in Alaska select their first choice candidate, followed by options to rank up to four other candidates in order of preference.

Industry observers note that "There is no specific law preventing people with the same name running, but many states have laws or regulations about how names appear on the ballot. One of those regulations was used in Alaska" remarked Ruth Greenwood, director of the election law clinic at Harvard Law School.

On Alaskans' ballots the two Sullivans were listed as:.

Industry observers note that - Sullivan, Dan S. (Registered Republican) Incumbent.

There was a second registered Republican candidate, Gerald Heikes - who was also allegedly recruited into the race according to The Fresh York Times.

A sample ballot for the US Senate election in Alaska.

As of Tuesday, Peltola holds 49.98% of the vote.

According to recent reports, in the event that Peltola were not to clear 50%, officials eliminate the candidate in last place and reallocate those ballots to the voters' next choices. This process continues until two candidates remain, with one clearing the 50% hurdle.

Daniel J Sullivan Jr is the listed candidate in last place with 1.65% of the vote.

Democrat Mary Peltola's stated on Saturday she will "decisively be elected" as Alaska's next senator.

Senator Dan S Sullivan and his allies have accused the Democrats of trying to confuse voters.

Trump mentioned last week: "Anybody that voted for that second Dan Sullivan, the fake Dan Sullivan, was supposed to be a vote for the real Dan Sullivan".

Of the ballots analysed by BBC Verify that ranked Daniel J Sullivan Jr first, 38% of them recorded no valid second choice.

We do not know how many of these voters may have thought they had voted for the Senator Dan S Sullivan and then not ranked any other candidates.

A further 29% of Daniel J Sullivan Jr voters ranked the Democratic candidate Mary Peltola second, almost double the 15% that ranked the incumbent Republican Senator Sullivan as second.

"The likelihood that any confusion might play a significant role is diminished in Alaska," Richard Pildes, a professor of constitutional law at New York University, argues, "because any voter who was unsure which Dan Sullivan candidate they meant to vote for could rank them first and second.".

Additional reporting by Daniel Wainwright.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

From train timetables to coffee cups and property underquoting, the NSW premier is making policy reversals well ahead of the March election.

Get our daily political email, free app or daily news podcast.

If recent coverage is to be believed, the Newly introduced South Wales premier, Chris Minns, is a talented gymnast. A last-minute intervention by the premier on Monday afternoon, the day before a suite of reforms on underquoting were due to take effect, marks a quadruple or quintuple policy “backflip” by Minns in recent weeks, depending on who you ask.

The laws banning real estate agents from lowering the advertised price of a property beneath a previously rejected written offer have been shelved for up to a year, after the premier flagged on Monday morning he had received concerns from estate agents in his own electorate about their effect amid a housing market downturn.

The NSW opposition leader, Kellie Sloane, remarked the move was “government by 2GB”, referencing the Sydney talkback radio station which had also raised the issue on Monday morning.

“But this isn’t the first time” she told presenter Ben Fordham on Tuesday.

First, the government backed down last month from implementing changes to several local and regional rail line timetables after criticism from commuters.

Next, after a social media post by Sloane, it changed gender-neutral language of “carer” and “lactating parents” in a upcoming parliamentary breastfeeding policy to reflect what Minns said was “commonsense language like ‘mother’ and ‘breastfeeding’”.

After the Daily Telegraph ran a “Nup to the Cup” campaign against plastics legislation, which included requiring cafes to offer dine-in customers mugs and glasses instead of takeaway cups, the government dropped the changes, which would not have been implemented until 2028.

This weekend, it made an election promise of a two-year funding guarantee for community preschools after the opposition had warned the sector was facing a $150m annual cut from January.

But Eamonn Fitzpatrick, a lobbyist and former communications and campaign advisor to federal and state Labor governments, notes the reversals are more about “clear air” than pre-campaign jitters as the government enters the final sitting days before the March election.

Recent findings suggest that “That is the job of this final sitting week, let’s not forget you go into summer. It’s a dead period,” claims Fitzpatrick, who worked alongside Minns in the office of former Labor premier Morris Iemma.

“What you’re seeking to do, actually, in either putting things on hold, changing your minds, revising policies, you’re actually just minimising distraction … clearing the runway.”.

Fitzpatrick says interventions are part of Minns’ brand as a strong leader, but insists his style is no more top-down than previous premiers.

Minns has consistently polled ahead of Sloane as preferred premier but he has made no secret about the threat from One Nation, whom he and his ministers have started to refer to as the state’s unofficial opposition.

Peter Lewis, the non-executive chair of strategic communications company Essential, which undertook qualitative research for Labor in the last federal election, stated recent polling suggested voting intention in November in NSW was at 27% for Labor, 26% for One Nation and 23% for the Coalition.

Lewis says he thinks the threat of One Nation in NSW is being “used to push the political debate towards the right and could be used as an excuse for the government not to embrace more progressive policies”.

“I wonder if there is a bit of a mistake in that. One Nation voters are being driven by dissatisfaction with the status quo and so governments that are seen as actually addressing issues probably have a better case to answer.”.

Defending its underquoting backflip, Labor has noted it is protecting buyers from being shut out of sales at lower prices amid a downturn which has seen home values in Sydney drop by 10.1% from their 2026 peak, according to data from Cotality.

In question time, the fair trading minister, Anoulack Chanthivong, whose department was responsible for the reforms and who has now been overruled for a third time by Minns on policy, said the market had changed and the government had responded.

Both he and Minns pointed out that Sloane and the opposition had supported the underquoting laws at the time, which were conceived for a “rising hot market”.

But, Lewis notes “there is a cost in being seen to change a position” – and points to Peter Dutton’s 2025 federal election campaign as an example.

“Maybe Minns has done this early enough in the cycle for it not to be an glitch, but as you get close to the election it changes, particularly when they’re walking back commitments that have been made to benefit people.

  • Later, they quit their jobs to join the startup accelerator Y Combinator, where they first tried out other ideas in areas like B2B and software-as-a-service, but weren’t finding the right fit.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that A new startup is taking a different approach to helping people manage their screen time. Instead of blocking apps or restricting the phone’s use after a set period, an app called Island encourages you to meet your screen time goals by way of a farming simulator game. Yes, a game! Island works by rewarding you when you’re disciplined enough to meet your goals with a “credit score” that increases your farm’s production, unlocking new crops, animals, and other content.

This carrot-instead-of-stick approach was dreamed up by entrepreneurs Ashish Selvaraj (CEO) and Ethan Pronev (CTO), who met while studying at the University of Waterloo, then went on to work at companies that included Jane Street, Citadel, Databricks, and Microsoft.

Later, they quit their jobs to join the startup accelerator Y Combinator, where they first tried out other ideas in areas like B2B and software-as-a-service, but weren’t finding the right fit.

Island ended up being their fifth pivot, and the first the founders actually found themselves enjoying.

“Once we were in YC, I think there’s a big mindset — I think in [San Francisco], in general — of, ‘selling shovels.’ Everyone wants to ‘sell shovels’ to other companies, and around us, that’s just what was going on,” explains Selvaraj, speaking about the concept that many successful startups sell the tools, infrastructure, or services to others following whatever the current market boom or trend may be.

“So all the ideas we had — we tried these things — but we found that we weren’t passionate about it. Like idea after idea seemed like ultimately the product was just a dashboard with some kind of different backend,” he added. “It felt like we quit our jobs … just to do something that was a variation of that.”.

With Island, the team gets to tap into their creativity, having drawn the pixel art themselves.

Recent findings suggest that “A lot of people do use [AI] models to generate the art, but we felt that it had a certain character when we drew it ourselves,” he told TechCrunch. “I feel like with Claude getting so good, there’s a tendency to give away every task to Claude. But ultimately it feels like there’s something else that comes out when you do it yourself, especially in something like art,” Selvaraj said.

What’s more, the app does appear to be successful in helping consumers meet their goals, the startup’s early data indicates. After early testing and an October launch, the team indicates that the majority of its users (82%) will end their screen time right at the limit they’ve set. Many more are ending their screen time when they get the “15 minutes left” warning.

Island could appeal to those who have given up on other screen time apps out of frustration because the app doesn’t actually lock you out of apps or your phone. That’s something that can end up being more disruptive, especially when you’re in the middle of doing something, like posting, sharing, commenting, or chatting, among other things. Instead, Island taps into owners’ own self-discipline and their desire to see their island flourish to encourage screen time breaks.

The idea to encourage customers to keep their goals by offering some other type of in-app reward system isn’t entirely novel. Last year, Hank Green’s screen time app Focus Friend went viral for its experience, which involved a little friend that could only knit items that, in turn, allowed you to get points used to decorate your room when you were focused on your non-distracting apps.

Similar ideas have been used in self-care apps and habit-trackers like Finch, Amaru, Belly, Flora, Urso, and others. But Island expands this concept from being focused on helping out a virtual friend or pet to one that’s more of a game — and one where you can experience the consequences without “having to torture your pet,” notes Selvaraj.

Island also allows users to add friends and visit each other’s islands, compete in group challenges, and keep each other accountable by tying your island together with one friend of your choosing. In the latter scenario, if either friend goes over their limit, both of their islands will suffer.

The startup claims Island has proven to be fairly “sticky” with a 51% daily active users-to-monthly active users ratio, and a day 30 retention rate of 49%, meaning 49% of users were still active on the app on the 30th day since the app was installed.

The app is right now free to use, with a $39.99 per year subscription that allows you to set individual limits on different apps, instead of just an overall daily screen time limit. The firm hasn’t raised additional seed funding outside of YC, but intends to begin marketing the app on social media for the rest of the year.

#12415. Breaking: Neurable One review: The brain-scanning headphones that helped me stay focused

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2200 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Engadget ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Neurable One review: The brain-scanning headphones that helped me stay focused

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2200 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The cans hide a wearable EEG that tracks your attention.
  • In a recent development, I've always been fascinated by the inner workings of the human mind, and I've tested plenty of brain gadgets in my time.
  • The company describes it as a "fitness tracker for your brain," so when your attention starts to drift, the headphones will remind you to keep your focus where it needs to be.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The cans hide a wearable EEG that tracks your attention.

In a recent development, I've always been fascinated by the inner workings of the human mind, and I've tested plenty of brain gadgets in my time. Sadly, all of them have been so clunky that they can only really be worn in the privacy of your own home. At least, that was the case. The Neurable One actually buries its brain-scanning technology into a pair of beefy over-ear headphones. It's designed to keep an eye on your focus levels and attention while you work, or meditate, wherever you are.

The company describes it as a "fitness tracker for your brain," so when your attention starts to drift, the headphones will remind you to keep your focus where it needs to be. And, if things continue to go wayward, you'll be advised to take a break and come back fresh rather than burning out halfway through the day. In that regard, it's been fascinating to see how the system thinks my brain operates on a regular basis.

According to recent reports, the Neurable One is cheaper than its predecessors and its competitors, and Neurable has improved its software platform. If there's a downside, it's that as much as I've loved my time with them, it's hard to think anyone other than nerds like me will want to use them.

Neurable spun out of a project from the University of Michigan in 2015, with the goal of building Brain Computer Interfaces (BCIs) and algorithms to interpret that data. The focus is on cognitive performance as there's plenty of military and civilian applications for the technology. Despite the name, Neurable One is actually the third pair of EEG headphones the company has made. In 2024, it partnered with Master & Dynamic on the MW75 Neuro, and a year later the Neuro LT, a lighter version of the same product addressing user comfort issues. This time out, Neurable is going it alone without the backing of any fancy audio brands.

In a recent development, at a glance, you'll struggle to notice much difference between this and its predecessors, as any variances are mostly aesthetic tweaks. Button placements are the same, but they're now pill-shaped rather than the circles found on the older models. The logo on the earcups has changed from M&D's icon to Neurable's signature brainwave, and there are fewer vents. In fact, the biggest difference is the loss of the cantilevered armatures joining the headband to the earcups, which have been replaced with standard hardware here.

It's a similar story inside the body as well; the Neurable One is more or less equipped with the same gear as before. You'll get the same 40mm Beryllium drivers, Bluetooth 5.2, AAC and aptX, albeit with six microphones — down from the eight on the MW75 Neuro. As before, each earcup has a series of dry-fit EEG sensors woven into the earpads which sit around your ear.

Neurable's pitch is to help people gain deeper insights into their own cognitive performance through the day. It contends that, much like the rest of our body, our minds have enough fuel to get us through the day, but not at full-tilt, full-pelt output. The tech giant notes it's a better idea to, when your attention and focus starts to wane, take a break ahead of you burning out. Neurable argues that spending a quick five minutes staring out of the window is better than getting a headache and not functioning for an hour.

Sources indicate that strap the headphones on at the start of the day and the system will keep an eye on how you're doing. Do this over a period of days, or weeks, and you'll get a sense of where your focus is at its highest and lowest. You can then adjust your working patterns to suit those stats. The Neurable One works equally well when you're meditating or relaxing, giving you insights as to how and when your mind rests.

Sources indicate that one of my eternal gripes with a lot of wearable EEGs (and other fabric sensors more broadly) is that the sensor pads are often fussy. They often don't work at all if they're bone dry and the skin they're in contact with is dry as well, which frustrates me. I've regularly had to gently dab the pads with cold water before running a washcloth across my forehead to dampen it. But, if the skin and pads are too wet, you'll be given a warning to dry both out, which slows you down even further. Thankfully, the Neurable One's dry-fit sensors worked from the get-go more or less every time I've used them. Every now and again, I'll be asked to push my (short) hair away from around my ears to improve the connection, but it's a world away from other products in the same field that I've tested.

Industry observers note that setup is a breeze, and the process of beginning your first session is relatively effortless, as is the daily routine you're expected to fall into. That begins with a check in at the start of the day, closing your eyes and triggering a 60-second scan of your brain. You'll get a dashboard containing your scores, with a comparison to the day before to see if things got better or worse. If you had a rough night, or if there's a lot going on, you can journal some notes on the same pane.

What's far more interesting and useful are the Insights and Improve sections, which tell you both what to do to manage your cognitive load right now, and how to boost it. The former suggests that you delay big decisions, not starting jobs that need a lot of attention and grouping small, repetitive tasks together. The latter asks you to go for a quick walk in the sun, go sit in another room away from your computer for five minutes or to write down all of the things sitting in your mental cache. Once done, you can run another check-in to see if that's made any improvement.

Industry observers note that if I'm honest, I was having a busy day at the start of a busy week, and felt snowed under by all of the projects on my desk. (In fact, my biggest concern, throughout testing these headphones, was that my Cognitive Load was always problematically high. It's almost as if working in journalism and juggling hundreds of projects all at once is somehow a problem.) The app told me that I was running low, but said I should walk up and down my stairs for a few minutes and then come back and check again. And, wouldn't you know, it actually did improve both my score and my ability to get stuff done for the rest of the morning.

Recent findings suggest that most days, I would set the EEG running at 9AM or so and not take them off until 12 or 1PM. The app will keep track of how well it thinks you're concentrating, letting you see that as a real time figure on screen. If it detects your focus beginning to drift, it'll rouse you back, but after a while, if you still struggle to concentrate, it'll advise you to take a short break. One thing I don't like is the way the system prods you to get back on track: When it thinks your focus is waning, you'll get a ping played in your ear as a sort of "come on, pay attention" trigger.

Industry observers note that it's a harsh noise, and one that would distract me as often as it did help me drift back toward focus. You can shut off this guidance in the app, but I persevered with them even when it put me in mind of a '70s kung fu B-movie where the protagonist is asked to build a house of cards while being pelted with rotten fruit. Regularly, I'd be halfway through writing a line in what I'd describe as a flow state and then I'd get pinged, knocking me off my train of thought.

But the more I used the headphones, the more I was able to see when the system remarked I was doing well and what caused slips. It became an increasingly positive feedback loop where I'd scrub through the timeline of my morning to see what I was doing when my focus was high.

According to recent reports, as for audio quality, it's clear the organization has tried to sail close to Master & Dynamic's promise of warm bass and clear treble. There's a wonderful atmosphere to the sound that makes you feel like you're in the room when it was recorded. One of my favourite tracks to test headphones with is "Finale" from the Tron: Legacy soundtrack where you can hear the horn player's breath. Wearing these, I was equally delighted to feel the rumble of the kettle drums pushing the air to my ear as they crescendoed.

The downside of Neurable no longer working with an established audio brand is that the One loses the added-value features inside the app. Whereas the previous models had a custom EQ you could fiddle with to your heart's content, here you just get the default tuning. That's not a bad thing as the audio quality here is certainly good enough, but I hope this feature can be added later. The other problem is that the app doesn't really have any sort of integration with your music app of choice, and instead will just play generic synthwave by default. Thankfully it will keep running in the background while you switch to Spotify to play actual music as you go.

Recent findings suggest that interestingly, the original MW75 Neuro weighed in at 338 grams, which was heavy enough to force the company into making a lighter version. The Neuro LT was said to be 12 percent lighter, and you would have hoped that the Neurable One would continue that trend. Instead, it's rated for 345 grams, making it slightly heavier than the original. (In fact, the only pair of significant-name cans that beats it for weight are the AirPods Max 2, which weigh in at 386.2 grams.) After a few hours of wearing the Neurable One on my head each day, I really became aware of their presence. I'll admit, I'm not an over-ears person, and so maybe those who are don't mind the sensation of having their ears pinned back for most of the day.

As for battery life, Neurable states the One will run for 22 hours, or 12 hours if you're using the EEG. When using the EEG, without ANC, I got just over 12 hours of use from the headphones before needing to head to the charger. On one hand, that's more than enough time on a charge, on the other, I'd be negligent if I didn't point out it's far below the standard for premium headphones.

In a recent development, at $499, Neurable One is a lot cheaper than the previous versions, and you get all of the insights and data on offer, without any additional paywall. There aren't many companies making consumer-grade EEG headphones, and so Neurable doesn't have much competition. The only real alternative is Brainbit which makes EEG cans for researchers, but I've asked, and it said it does sell its headphones to consumers as well. They will set you back $900, and come with a free iOS, macOS, Android or Windows app to help you monitor your mind.

It has been revealed that naturally, if you're looking for a wearable EEG that isn't built into headphones, then you also have the option of Muse. Its latest is the Muse S Athena, an EEG headband designed to help improve your meditation, but it can also monitor your brain's oxygenation levels. It'll set you back $539 with a year of Muse's premium, which adds in data about your Alpha Peak and Brain Recharge, plus it integrates with Spotify, Calm or your audiobook player of choice.

If you'd rather just buy a pair of high-end headphones, you should instead head to Engadget's guide to the best on the market. It should go without saying that you can pick up plenty of better headphones for less — including Sony's class-leading XM6s.

I've spent a lot of time second-guessing my own recommendation, because on its own merits this is a great product. It does what it promises in an easy to use, accessible way and it's far cheaper than its (handful of) competitors. In that vacuum, it's well worth the cash, and I think I've meaningfully benefited from my time with this device. If you can afford it, and you're truly keen on learning more about how your own brain works, then I think it's worth it.

Recent findings suggest that the caveat here is that it really does need to be people who are committed to doing this work on a regular basis. I suspect we're a generation or two away from a version of these cans which are truly usable by the mainstream more broadly.

Industry News: US moves to cut China’s remote access to AI chips

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1258 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • On the heels of the Nvidia scandal, the Trump administration is preparing to crack down on foreign data centers that are fueling China’s advancements in artificial intelligence by allowing remote access to otherwise restricted high-end chips necessary for AI training.
  • In a summary of the rule change, the Commerce Department noted it was closing a loophole that previously allowed foreign rivals like China, Russia, and Iran to bypass export curbs on certain advanced computer chips by instead renting access to those chips from data centers in Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Brazil.
  • In a recent development, US rivals could possibly use that access to train and run advanced AI models “capable of supporting military- and intelligence-related activities that could threaten US national security or foreign policy interests,” the Commerce Department said.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On the heels of the Nvidia scandal, the Trump administration is preparing to crack down on foreign data centers that are fueling China’s advancements in artificial intelligence by allowing remote access to otherwise restricted high-end chips necessary for AI training.

In a summary of the rule change, the Commerce Department noted it was closing a loophole that previously allowed foreign rivals like China, Russia, and Iran to bypass export curbs on certain advanced computer chips by instead renting access to those chips from data centers in Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Brazil.

In a recent development, US rivals could possibly use that access to train and run advanced AI models “capable of supporting military- and intelligence-related activities that could threaten US national security or foreign policy interests,” the Commerce Department said. Among threats, the US fears rivals could use advanced AI to develop “more effective weapons of mass destruction and advanced conventional weapons, coordinated cyber-espionage and targeted cyber-disruption, algorithmic theft, and weaponized disinformation.”.

Now, the rules have been tightened up so much that the South China Morning Post reported that, “as a result, any advanced chips made for a Chinese firm are assumed to be restricted, and factories must ask the US government for a license before shipping them.”.

The rule change takes effect 90 days after it’s posted to the Federal Register. Moving forward, companies headquartered in any of those countries deemed to “present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion” to China, Russia, and Iran must apply for a license with strict know-your-customer controls when transferring high volumes of advanced chips. If a license is granted, companies will have to “perform robust due diligence,” submitting monthly reports on transactions that thoroughly detail all parties involved, as well as their parent companies, and the final destination for chips sold.

In a press release Sunday, the Commerce Department described the rule change as “designed to ensure that existing restrictions on access to sensitive American technology cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements involving data centers in third countries.” An exception was carved out for companies providing computing power “exclusively used for commercial recommender systems.” The Department noted it was acting to “prevent certain foreign actors from leveraging advanced computing power based on US technology to threaten US national security and foreign policy interests.”.

Without the intervention, officials fear that China could develop a military or economic edge, The Upcoming York Times reported.

Recent findings suggest that nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned after admitting to an affair with a woman, Alice Huang, suspected of serving as a Chinese spy. Congress is probing if Alice Huang used her personal relationship with Jensen Huang to help her former tech giant, Megaspeed, become one of Nvidia’s biggest customers, then used that position to smuggle Nvidia’s restricted AI chips into China. China has denied that Alice Huang was a spy, and Megaspeed has denied that smuggling occurred, while launching its own internal probe.

In a recent development, megaspeed is a Singaporean data center firm whose primary business is cloud computing and AI infrastructure. Prior to the rule change, selling remote access to AI servers to customers in China was perfectly legal, NYT noted. But now, the Commerce Department has given firms like Megaspeed 90 days to either obtain licenses or face future export restrictions.

In a recent development, whether or not to add more chip curbs has been a polarizing debate in the Trump administration. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent reportedly butted heads with Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick. When the Megaspeed news broke, Bessent pushed for curbs, but Lutnick reportedly appeared “too cozy” with Nvidia to move. Instead, Lutnick initially favored looser controls that Nvidia claimed would ensure global dominance of US technology. (A Commerce Department spokesperson told NYT that Bessent has never confronted Lutnick over his handling of Megaspeed.).

In a recent development, any companies found violating the rules could face a “range of consequences,” the Commerce Department said after reportedly bending to Bessent’s pressure campaign. Those include possibly facing new import restrictions, stricter license requirements, downgrading their status in the US export control regime, or other changes to their organization’s or their base country’s entity-list designations.

Although the summary of the rule change said that “Commerce will be actively monitoring for countries that tolerate evasion” of the anti-diversion policy, it’s unclear how aggressively the Commerce Department might enforce the rule, NYT noted.

Bessent has publicly criticized Lutnick for failing to sanction Megaspeed, and NYT reported that ultimately, enforcement of the stricter rules—which Bessent helped draft—“would be up to the Commerce Department.”.

“The real story here should be: Did Nvidia know their client, and was there a robust effort at Nvidia to make sure that there was no leakage and that they were selling to what were obviously pass-through shell companies?” Bessent noted on a CNBC appearance. “I think it’s vital that anyone at the company there be held accountable for that.”.

In a recent development, there’s even a push to oust Lutnick over his position on chips, but The Guardian reported that Donald Trump confirmed he has no prepares to replace the AI industry-friendly commerce secretary. On Monday, Trump told reporters that Lutnick was right to delay blacklisting Megaspeed, because “if you didn’t delay it… you could have a blow-up with China.”.

In a recent development, at the press gaggle, Trump aligned with China in saying that there’s no evidence yet that Alice Huang was a spy. He also joined a band of prominent tech leaders calling for Jensen Huang’s return to Nvidia, saying that it wasn’t a “bad idea.”.

According to recent reports, “Nobody’s proven that she’s a spy,” Trump said. “She may not be a spy.”.

However, US investigators have alleged that they found “Alice Huang used industry contacts and a series of shell companies to access 240,000 chips banned for export into China,” CBS News reported.

China is unlikely to welcome the upcoming rules, as it has consistently accused the US of fabricating the spying claims to justify imposing additional chip restrictions.

However, a senior Trump official, granted anonymity to discuss sensitive policy matters, told the NYT that Trump “did not expect countermeasures from China in response.”.

According to recent reports, trump will be in China for an economic summit this week, including a meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping. The new curbs could potentially disrupt those talks, according to Hong Yuan, a researcher and secretary-general of the Center for American Military Studies at the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences. Hong told the People’s Daily that China will likely view the rule change as politically motivated.

“Before any judicial causality was established, Washington handed down a political conviction, substituting suspicion for proof, espionage for personal contact, and an industrial embargo for private conduct,” Hong mentioned. “The concern is not the cause of tighter controls, but a political catalyst.”.

The fresh policy could hurt the US, experts told the Chinese outlets. Analysts told the South China Morning Post that the policy could “accelerate Chinese companies’ shift to domestic AI chips.” Other experts told the People’s Daily—which is the official newspaper of the Chinese Communist Party—that “the cost of switching back to US platforms will rise” over time. If that happened, it could potentially lock in Chinese technology over America’s in “the world’s largest single consumer market for chips,” experts stated.

Sun Chenghao, senior fellow at the Center for International Security and Strategy at Tsinghua University in Beijing, told the People’s Daily that “what US companies stand to lose could be customers and technological influence for years to come.”.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Grand Theft Auto fans have waited 13 long years for the latest edition of the game to be released - and going to extreme lengths to be ready for its launch.
