    #12297. Windows 11 actually runs better on 8GB of RAM now

    📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1009 w)
    📖 Baca
    General 📈 Bullish 🌐 The Verge ↗ Open Full Page

    Windows 11 actually runs better on 8GB of RAM now

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1009 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: The Verge

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • I retested the base Surface Laptop, and Microsoft’s optimizations seem to be working.
    • I retested the base Surface Laptop, and Microsoft’s optimizations seem to be working.
    • Recent findings suggest that as recently as the beginning of the year, 16GB of RAM was common on sub-$800 Windows laptops, which helped compensate for an increasingly bloated-feeling Windows 11.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    I retested the base Surface Laptop, and Microsoft’s optimizations seem to be working.

    I retested the base Surface Laptop, and Microsoft’s optimizations seem to be working.

    Recent findings suggest that as recently as the beginning of the year, 16GB of RAM was common on sub-$800 Windows laptops, which helped compensate for an increasingly bloated-feeling Windows 11. But with the cost of RAM skyrocketing this year, 8GB is once again typical for a starting configuration. The MacBook Neo got away with it, but Windows laptops, including Microsoft’s own 13-inch Surface Laptop, could struggle. Microsoft was talking a big game about making Windows faster and more reliable before the RAM crisis really hit, and it now seems like that effort is beginning to bear fruit.

    Sources indicate that earlier this month, Pavan Davuluri, Microsoft’s EVP of Windows and devices, detailed in a blog post the improvements the manufacturer has made to Windows 11 to address the constraints of 8GB PCs. In it, Davuluri claims, “Windows is now up to 20% more responsive, and multitasking is up to 40% faster in our lab test.”.

    Sources indicate that the most significant change is in memory management. When there isn’t enough available memory to handle all active data, some of it has to be offloaded (or “paged out”) to storage. And SSDs, especially in lower-cost laptops, are much slower than RAM.

    When Windows needs to access data that’s been paged out from the RAM to the SSD, it’s called a hard fault (or page fault). If it happens a lot — say, on a laptop with only 8GB of RAM — it leads to little slowdowns like browser tabs requiring a refresh before you can access them again. Davuluri says, “Windows can now keep up to 2 GB more of your active data in memory instead of moving it to slower storage, so an app or tab you left open is less likely to reload when you return.”.

    Recent findings suggest that to test this, I fired up the same 13-inch Surface Laptop with 8GB of RAM that I reviewed back in July, when I proclaimed eight is not enough for Windows. This laptop was one of the worst examples of RAMageddon’s current stranglehold on computing: With half the RAM of last year’s base model, it struggled to keep up with my regular workload. And this is Microsoft’s hardware.

    Microsoft’s own laptop could struggle.

    Recent findings suggest that before updating the Surface to the latest Windows 11 build, I got reacquainted with this laptop and the version of Windows I left it on (25H2, build 26200.8875). It was rough. Running about 20 tabs (on the latest Chrome build) while streaming a 4K YouTube video and using Slack and Signal made everything from clicking tabs to swiping around Windows with trackpad gestures feel sluggish. Chrome tabs and apps would refresh after leaving them in the background for just a short moment. When you’re multitasking and bouncing between many tabs, like when researching something, those refreshes get incredibly frustrating. And the fan was running audibly the whole time. Keeping the Resource Monitor open demonstrated memory hard faults ranging from just under 700 faults per second to 29,000 faults per second, during which Windows ground to a halt. Seeing this number literally go off its chart showed just how badly Windows 11 struggled with memory management on 8GB before the patch.

    Now, after updating the Surface Laptop to Windows 11 version 26H2, build 26300.9974 (memory improvements are live on build 26300.9818 and beyond) things are much improved. I opened over 30 Chrome tabs while streaming the same 4K YouTube video and running the same chat apps, and Windows slowed a bit, but nowhere near as much. I could feel things like Task View get a little less responsive and at times stuttery, but it was the way you’d expect when taxing a system. Chrome tabs required less frequent refreshes. The fan also took longer to kick in and ran a little quieter and for shorter durations when it did.

    Recent findings suggest that taking a fresh look at the Resource Monitor, hard faults at normal operation were now under 300 per second, with occasional jumps to about 1,000. Performance was even slightly better when I subbed out Chrome for Microsoft Edge. Edge felt more responsive under load and had fewer hard faults when running 30 tabs, the same 4K YouTube video, and a Google Meet video call.

    I’m happy to see that the 8GB Surface Laptop now performs better, and I’m equally relieved that Windows 11 is starting to feel more viable on 8GB of RAM. (It’s still a shame the 8GB Surface Laptop costs more than last year’s 16GB, but I digress.) Do I want 8GB of RAM in any laptop I’m personally buying? No.

    As I said when I reviewed the latest Dell XPS 13, I appreciate that 8GB is workable — and it should be fine for basic needs today — but I still advise getting 16GB if you’re able. The extra headroom will keep things speedy for longer, especially after you bog a computer down with lots of files, apps, or games. And as much better as the 8GB Surface Laptop is now, I still managed to crash Chrome entirely with fewer than three dozen tabs. Microsoft has done better by its entry-level laptop, but it’s not a miracle worker.

    Sources indicate that our ongoing RAMageddon makes living with lower quantities of memory a grim reality. Microsoft is partly to blame for that, of course. And it hasn’t done itself any favors with all the feature bloat it put into Windows 11 during the Copilot / AI era. Meanwhile, other OSes, like Linux, macOS, and ChromeOS, can get by better with less. Still, I’m glad to see Microsoft ever so slightly right the ship in this one way.

    The seven-time Formula One world champion has spoken out about conflict and humanitarian crises in the region, and has called for peace. He has frequently posted on social media about children killed in Israeli airstrikes in Gaza and called for a ceasefire.

    Israeli forces have continued to advance, expanding their control from 53% of the territory to at least 60%, an independent commission of UN experts remarked last month.

    Airstrikes also continue, and Israeli fire along the advancing front has killed at least 196 Palestinians, including 18 women, 32 boys and 11 girls, the commission remarked.

    Hamilton toured Egypt’s Rafah border crossing with Gaza before visiting logistics warehouses operated by the Egyptian Red Crescent, which facilitates the entry of aid to Gaza.

    At the crossing, Hamilton greeted aid workers with “Assalamu alaikum” a widely used Arabic greeting meaning “peace be upon you.” He shook hands and briefly spoke to workers and officials.

    Khaled Megawer, the governor of North Sinai, where Rafah is located, said the visit was intended to help Hamilton learn about Egypt’s efforts to send aid to Gaza.

    The visit comes after Hamilton made his 400th race start on Sunday at the São Paulo Grand Prix at Interlagos.

    It has been revealed that the first black F1 driver, he made his debut with McLaren in 2007. He is only the second F1 driver to start 400 races after his former teammate Fernando Alonso, who achieved the milestone in 2024.

    A funeral was held for Fadwa al-Fahidat in the village of al-Duyuk al-Tahta on Tuesday.

    A Palestinian woman in her 70s has been shot dead, and several other people wounded, in a village in the occupied West Bank where Israeli settlers recently moved in, the Palestinian health ministry says.

    In a recent development, there are conflicting accounts of what happened. Local Palestinians noted there was an attack by settlers in part of al-Duyuk al-Tahta, near Jericho, which is meant to be under the full control of the Palestinian Authority.

    Recent findings suggest that according to the Israeli army, there was a Palestinian car-ramming attack on an Israeli vehicle. It stated rocks were then thrown at the Israelis, who opened fire in response. It did not mention the fatal shooting of a woman.

    There have been high tensions in the area since a group of settlers recently set up a new outpost.

    They moved into eight houses in the village on 4 November after buying them, they have noted, in a secretive operation. The properties are in an area where Israel retains full security control.

    All settlements are illegal under international law.

    Medics say Palestinians and Israelis were wounded in the incident on Monday evening.

    Palestinian reports said Fadwa al-Fahidat, who was 72, was shot outside her home on Monday evening and that, hearing the news, her son sped to the scene in his car.

    He then collided with an empty Israeli vehicle parked outside his family home and settlers standing nearby were injured, they said. The settlers then began shooting, the reports said.

    The statement from the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said that "terrorists accelerated their vehicle toward an Israeli vehicle and rammed it", and then "exited their vehicle with weapons and attacked and harmed the occupants of the Israeli vehicle".

    Afterwards, it remarked, "rocks were hurled at the Israelis, who responded by firing in order to remove the threat.".

    The IDF remarked that Israeli security forces were sent to the scene and were pursuing suspects.

    Industry observers note that doctors at a hospital in Jericho stated that al-Fahidat was shot in the head. Several other Palestinians and Israelis were injured, reports said.

    The Israeli human rights group B'Tselem claims there has been a prolonged campaign of settler attacks, intimidation and land seizures in al-Duyuk al-Tahta, with Israeli troops now stationed nearby to secure the newly introduced settlement.

    Residents and activists say armed settlers walk and drive quad bikes around the neighbourhood as they threaten Palestinian residents.

    A group of settlers set up a latest outpost in al-Duyuk al-Tahta earlier this month (file photo).

    In a separate incident on Monday evening, eight Palestinians were injured when they were hit by a vehicle driven by an Israeli settler on a main road in Tuqu, south of Bethlehem, according to Palestinian officials and the Palestinian Red Crescent.

    The IDF said the incident was a traffic accident. But the Palestinian foreign ministry called it a "terrorist attack", saying the driver hit a group of Palestinians who had gathered near the scene of an earlier traffic accident.

    Also on Monday, the Civil Administration - the body that implements Israeli government policy in the West Bank - declared the allocation of more than 28 sq km (6,945 acres) of land in the northern Jordan Valley to nine settlers for grazing, according to the Israeli anti-settlement watchdog Peace Now.

    It said handing over vast tracts of land to settlers for grazing outposts constituted "direct support for the systematic expulsion of Palestinians from their lands and the rampant criminal violence in the West Bank".

    The UK government said on Tuesday that it was imposing sanctions on eight companies building Israeli settlements in the West Bank.

    It is the first sanctions package since Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband's pledge in September to respond to the accelerating rate of settlement expansion in the West Bank, which he remarked risked rendering a two-state solution unviable.

    Fabrice Koli, 5, at an Ebola treatment center in the town of Nizi, Democratic Republic of Congo, this summer after his 17-year-old brother died.Credit...

    Matthew Mpoke Bigg and Arlette Bashizi spent more than a week reporting on the Ebola outbreak from the town of Nizi, in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo.

    Gorette Mbusi stood on her doorstep and wrestled with a question. Should she let her grandson be taken to the hospital?

    In a recent development, health workers had come to her village, in the eastern part of the Democratic Republic of Congo, to implore her to let them take the young man to a specialized Ebola facility in the nearby town of Nizi. But she was wary. She had already lost two family members, including her daughter, who had been transported to the hospital and then died.

    “I don’t know where this sickness is coming from that is killing my family,” she remarked. “I feel abandoned.”.

    Recent findings suggest that ms. Mbusi’s dilemma reflects a central challenge for health workers as they struggle to contain the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak on record — how to stop people from passing the disease to loved ones at home.

    Recent findings suggest that community transmission happens when family members care for Ebola patients at home and then become ill themselves, spreading the disease and making it more difficult for medical teams to identify and isolate people who have been in contact with those infected. Tracking and tracing the contacts of Ebola patients and educating people about the virus are crucial to ending community transmission.

    Health workers must first get more people to seek medical treatment in hospitals sooner and overcome deep suspicions about Ebola in villages like this one, known as Nizi 4.

    Isomorphic Labs raises $5B as it looks to take drug candidates to clinical trials

    ⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Isomorphic Labs, the AI drug-discovery platform that was spun out of Google’s DeepMind in 2021, has raised $5 billion in a Series C funding round as it seeks to take its drug candidates to clinical trials.
    • The funding was co-led by Greenoaks and Sequoia Capital, with upcoming investor Andreessen Horowitz and other investors also participating.
    • In a recent development, isomorphic Labs builds an AI drug-design engine that uses a slew of simulation AI models that explore various areas of chemistry to help the company design drugs.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Isomorphic Labs, the AI drug-discovery platform that was spun out of Google’s DeepMind in 2021, has raised $5 billion in a Series C funding round as it seeks to take its drug candidates to clinical trials.

    The funding was co-led by Greenoaks and Sequoia Capital, with upcoming investor Andreessen Horowitz and other investors also participating. All of the firm’s existing backers, including Alphabet’s venture divisions GV and Capital G, Thrive Capital, MGX, Temasek, and the UK Sovereign AI Fund, also invested.

    In a recent development, isomorphic Labs builds an AI drug-design engine that uses a slew of simulation AI models that explore various areas of chemistry to help the company design drugs. The company, whose work builds on DeepMind’s breakthrough AlphaFold protein-folding AI model, said its program has yielded “positive preclinical results” in oncology and immunology. The lab has struck deals with pharma giants like Eli Lilly, Novartis, and Johnson & Johnson.

    The new funding, which comes on the heels of a $2.1 billion Series B round in May, will be used to continue developing its drug-design engine, as well as to foray into more types of medicine.

    The Series C is Isomorphic’s first fundraise since its founder and CEO, Demis Hassabis, left his position as head of DeepMind to focus on drug discovery, which also saw him moving into a chairman role at DeepMind. Hassabis and then-director of DeepMind John Jumper won the Nobel Prize in chemistry for the lab’s work on AlphaFold, a system that predicts the 3D structure of proteins with nothing more than their genetic sequence.

    Isomorphic did not disclose its upcoming valuation. Bloomberg reported earlier this month that the lab was looking to raise funding at a $50 billion valuation.

    Sources indicate that amazon no longer considers the midrange Fire TV Stick 4K Plus as part of its official lineup following the launch of it latest Fire TV Stick 4K, but that doesn’t mean the streaming device isn’t still good value. In fact, it’s an even more attractive option now that it’s dropped to $29.99 ($40 off) at Amazon and Best Buy in the run-up to Black Friday. That’s just $5 shy of its lowest price to date, rendering it cheaper than both the entry-level Fire TV Stick HD and its newly introduced midrange replacement, the Fire TV Stick 4K.

    The Fire TV Stick 4K Plus still offers a good balance of price and performance. Unlike its replacement, it supports both Dolby Vision and Dolby Atmos, delivering more vibrant colors, better contrast, and immersive audio with compatible TVs and speakers. It does require a separate power adapter, though, whereas the newer model can draw power directly from your TV’s USB port. You also don’t get as much storage here as with the high-end Fire TV Stick 4K Max, though 8GB should be plenty for streaming apps like Netflix and Disney Plus.

    The Plus model also supports Amazon’s redesigned Fire TV interface, which my colleague John Higgins found to be an impressive patch. It makes it easier to browse different content categories and pin your favorite apps for quick access. Thanks to Alexa Plus support, you can also press the voice button on the included Alexa Voice Remote to find something to watch, control compatible smart home devices like lights and thermostats, check sports scores, and more without getting off your couch. Just don’t expect a customizable shortcut button, as that’s exclusive to the latest Fire TV Remote.

    One final note: the Plus ships with Amazon’s Fire OS, and unlike the tech giant’s Vega OS that ships in newer streaming sticks, the former allow for sideloading of Android TV apps, if that’s of interest to you.
